Case study: Isle de Jean Charles Resettlement (Isle de Jean Charles, Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana, USA)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Isle de Jean Charles (IDJC) Resettlement — Isle de Jean Charles, Terrebonne Parish, coastal Louisiana, United States of America.

**Hazard(s):** The primary hazards driving retreat are coastal land loss through erosion and subsidence, sea-level rise, chronic flooding of the sole access road (Island Road), and hurricane storm surge. These hazards interact in a compounding relationship: subsidence exacerbates flooding, storm surge accelerates erosion, and the loss of protective wetlands amplifies all impacts. They are driven by natural processes and substantially accelerated by anthropogenic factors — particularly levee construction that cut off Mississippi River sediment replenishment, and oil and gas extraction that carved canals through wetlands and caused additional subsidence and saltwater intrusion (Jessee 2022; Birch et al. 2024).

**Type of Retreat:** Community resettlement — a structured, voluntary relocation of the Island's permanent residents and displaced former residents to a newly developed inland site ("The New Isle"), approximately 40 miles north of Isle de Jean Charles, near Schriever in Terrebonne Parish. The program combines individual household assistance with community-scale master planning. It departs from standard HUD buyout models by allowing residents to retain ownership of their Island properties for cultural, recreational, and ceremonial use rather than requiring title transfer and demolition (OCD 2020a; OCD 2021).

**Scale:** As of the Phase I census (October 2016), 26 active residential units housed 37 households and 99 total residents on the Island (OCD 2017). The program materials identify up to 42 eligible households across current and displaced former residents across multiple option types (OCD 2020b). The New Isle spans approximately 515 acres — some documents reference 508 acres, reflecting the surveyed parcel configuration prior to final transaction — and is planned for approximately 120 residential lots plus commercial, community, and recreational uses (OCD 2020a; OCD 2021).

**Key Actors:** The primary implementing agency is the Louisiana Office of Community Development (OCD), Disaster Recovery Unit, which administers a $48.3 million federal grant from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), awarded through the National Disaster Resilience Competition (NDRC) (OCD 2017; OCD 2021). The Isle de Jean Charles Band of Biloxi-Chitimacha-Choctaw (BCC) Tribal leadership and the Lowlander Center (a nonprofit founded in 2010 and incorporated in 2013) were foundational to the original resettlement vision and contributed to the successful NDRC grant application (Jessee 2022). The United Houma Nation (UHN) also has members on the Island. Key planning partners included CSRS (prime engineering consultant), Waggonner & Ball (architecture), OLIN (landscape architecture), the Center for Planning Excellence (community engagement), and others (OCD 2021). The Louisiana Land Trust (LLT) acquired the New Isle site on behalf of the state and serves as development partner (OCD 2021).

**Timeline:** The BCC Tribe began planning inland resettlement in approximately 2002 after the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers excluded the Island from regional hurricane protection (Jessee 2022; Simms et al. 2021). The Lowlander Center was founded in 2010 and incorporated in 2013 as a nonprofit collaborating with Tribal leaders (Jessee 2022). Louisiana received the HUD NDRC grant on January 25, 2016 (OCD 2017). Phase I (data gathering and engagement) ran June–November 2016. Phase II (site selection, acquisition, and master planning) ran December 2016–February 2019. The LLT purchased the Evergreen site on December 28, 2018; the master plan received unanimous Terrebonne Parish Planning Commission approval on February 21, 2019 (OCD 2021). The formal program launched on March 9, 2019 (OCD 2020b). Infrastructure construction began in May 2020. Houses were under construction in 2021, with move-in expected in 2022; as of the most recent sources, the resettlement remains ongoing in Phase III (OCD 2021; Soundararajan 2022).

**Key Outcomes:** The New Isle site was purchased, master-planned, and is under construction. Between the program's July 2017 launch and March 2019, 20 households moved into off-island rental housing through the Optional Relocation Assistance (ORA) program; the Phase 2 Report states "nearly 20 island families" were in ORA-funded rental units as of that report's coverage period (OCD 2021). By the later sources, 37 of 42 eligible households had applied to participate (Simms et al. 2021). The program introduced an innovative policy allowing residents to retain ownership of Island properties for non-residential use, explicitly described as "a significant departure from traditional HUD-funded relocation programs" (OCD 2020a; OCD 2021; Simms et al. 2021). However, the process was significantly marked by conflict between the state and BCC Tribal leadership. Jessee (2022) argues that the state systematically transformed the Tribal-driven resettlement — originally framed as cultural survival and self-determination — into a scalable "managed retreat" model, erasing Indigenous planning, weakening commitments to Tribal identity and governance, and failing to honor its partnership with the Tribe. Broader Louisiana coastal planning (the Coastal Master Plans and LA SAFE initiative) increasingly recognized managed retreat as a necessary adaptation strategy but — as Birch et al. (2024) document — produced only limited, largely non-scaled relocation action, without developing the social infrastructure or governance structures necessary to implement it systematically.

---

### Narrative Summary

Isle de Jean Charles is a narrow strip of land in the southernmost Louisiana bayou, once encompassing over 22,000 acres and home to a community of predominantly American Indian ancestry — primarily members of the Isle de Jean Charles Band of Biloxi-Chitimacha-Choctaw (BCC) Tribe and the United Houma Nation. For over a century, the Island has been disappearing: subsidence from natural deltaic processes has combined with levee construction (which cut off sediment replenishment from the Mississippi River) and oil and gas extraction (which carved canals through wetlands, enabling saltwater intrusion and causing additional subsidence) to reduce the Island from over 22,000 acres to approximately 320 acres remaining (OCD 2020a; Jessee 2022). The Island's sole road floods regularly, cutting residents off from jobs, schools, and health care. After the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers excluded the Island from regional hurricane protection in 2002 based on a cost-benefit analysis that found protection extension unjustified, BCC Tribal leaders began planning an inland resettlement as "an act of cultural survival" — intending not simply to move houses, but to reunite a displaced Tribe, preserve heritage, and create a teaching and learning community (Jessee 2022).

In January 2016, HUD awarded Louisiana $48.3 million through the NDRC to implement the Isle de Jean Charles Resettlement — the first federally funded, community-scale, climate-driven resettlement in the United States. The state's OCD took the lead, conducting extensive community engagement over multiple phases, purchasing approximately 515 acres of farmland near Schriever, developing a detailed master plan in collaboration with residents, and beginning construction of "The New Isle." The program offered eligible households either a new home at The New Isle (Option A), homebuyer assistance toward an existing home elsewhere in Louisiana (Option D), or an improved lot at the new site (Option B). A key innovation was allowing residents to retain ownership of their Island properties for cultural and recreational use, after residents made clear that demolition and title transfer were non-negotiable conditions of their non-participation (Simms et al. 2021; OCD 2020a).

The process was, however, deeply contested. Jessee (2022) documents — through five years of ethnographic research alongside Tribal leaders — how the state progressively transformed the Tribal-driven resettlement into a more generic managed-retreat model: opening eligibility broadly under Fair Housing Act rationale, replacing a planned Tribal community center with a parish recreation center, prioritizing individual property transfers over communal land ownership, erasing pre-NDRC Tribal planning from public timelines, and reducing commitments to Tribal identity, sovereignty, and reunification. Tribal leaders described this as a "bait and switch," likening it to historical colonial land dispossession (Jessee 2022; Soundararajan 2022). Meanwhile, broader Louisiana coastal planning — analyzed by Birch et al. (2024) across the 2007, 2012, 2017, and 2023 Coastal Master Plans and the LA SAFE framework — increasingly recognized managed retreat as a necessary adaptation strategy, but consistently failed to develop the actionable governance structures, social infrastructure, or sustained funding mechanisms needed to implement relocation at scale. As of early 2022, house construction at The New Isle was nearing completion, but significant uncertainty remained about Tribal futures, community cohesion, and whether the process could serve as a replicable model for other communities.

Case study: Shaanxi Ecological Resettlement (Shaanxi Province, China)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Massive Southern Shaanxi Migration Program (MSSMP), implemented at the provincial scale across southern Shaanxi Province, northwest China, with primary case study focus on Shangnan County (Shangluo Municipality). The program also encompasses Ankang and Hanzhong Municipalities. Shangnan County is located in the Qin-ba mountain region and is crossed from west to east by the Danjiang River [1][3].

**Hazard(s):** The main hazards cited across sources are flooding, flood-induced landslides and debris flows, and drought, alongside severe soil erosion and ecological fragility in steep mountainous terrain. These hazards occur in a context of regional climate trends (increasing temperatures, increased extreme rainfall events), though the program is also motivated by poverty alleviation and watershed protection goals that are distinct from direct disaster causation [1][2][3][4]. Sources document that between 1997 and 2012, five droughts and seven floods and flood-induced landslides occurred in Shangnan County — twice the rate of the prior 16-year period [1]. More than 2,000 geologic hazard events occurred across the three-municipality program area between 2001 and 2010, causing 590 deaths and 7.1 billion yuan in economic losses [4].

**Type of Retreat:** Government-initiated resettlement program (Government Resettlement Project — GRP). The program is described in the literature as ecological resettlement with poverty-alleviation goals [1][2][4]. Three relocation modes are available to eligible households: urban resettlement (go-into-city), scattered (dispersed) resettlement, and centralized (community) resettlement [2][5]. Participation is formally voluntary, with subsidies as incentives, though practical pressures are documented [1][3].

**Scale:** The MSSMP targets 2.4 million people (600,000 households) across 28 counties in three municipalities over a 10-year period (2011–2020) [1][2][4][5]. In Shangnan County, the target was 24,604 households (93,400 people); in the program's first year alone, Shangnan resettled over 2,100 households (7,991 people) [1]. In the Ankang Prefecture, the program aims to move 226,000 rural households (approximately 876,000 local residents) [2]. By the end of 2016, over 1.1 million people had been relocated across the program area [4].

**Key Actors:** The Shaanxi Provincial Government initiated and funds the MSSMP, formulating policies and guidelines [1]. Shangluo (municipal-level) and Shangnan/Ankang (county-level) governments propose candidate townships and villages, select eligible households, and manage implementation [1]. The Shangnan Poverty Alleviation and Resettlement Office (SPARO) administers the program at county level [1]. Township governments obtain construction approvals from multiple county departments (Land Resource Management Bureau, Forestry Bureau, Water Conservancy Bureau, and Construction and Housing Bureau) [1]. Village cadres play a critical frontline role in mobilizing and informing residents [1][3]. Academic researchers from Xi'an Jiaotong University, Stanford University, and Charles Sturt University have contributed evaluation studies, though these are research outputs rather than program governance functions [1][2][4].

**Timeline:** The MSSMP was formally launched by the Shaanxi Provincial Government in 2011 as a 10-year program (2011–2020) [1][2][5]. Shangnan County was selected as a pilot area from 2011 onwards, though Shangnan had run preceding GRPs since 1998 [1][3]. At the time of the primary research sources (2012–2017/2018), the program was actively underway. By the end of 2016, over 1.1 million people had been relocated across the program area [4]. The literature recommends further follow-up support and evaluation for subsequent program phases [2][4].

**Key Outcomes:**
- Significant improvement in housing quality, infrastructure access (electricity, running water, flush toilets, reduced distance to town/road/school) for resettled households [4].
- Livelihood transformation from traditional agriculture toward non-farm activities; increased income, though the net income gain is modest and total expenditure — especially housing construction — substantially exceeds income gains, leaving many households in debt [2][4].
- Multi-dimensional poverty reduced: number of poverty dimensions reduced by approximately 2.17 on average among participating households [4].
- Ecological service assessments projected improvements in sediment retention, nitrogen and phosphorus retention, and carbon sequestration; 2,267 ha of homestead and sloping farmland restored to forest and grass cover in the Ankang program area [2].
- Large reductions in the number of people suffering disasters, damaged crop area, and collapsed houses documented across the three municipalities between 2011 and 2015 [4].
- Persistent concerns: the poorest households are often excluded because an unofficial financial eligibility criterion requires sufficient household savings for relocation costs [1][3]; scarcity of farmland in receiving communities and difficulty reallocating farmland [2]; financial debt burdens for resettled households; livelihood transformation challenges; social network disruption [1][2][4].
- Some resettlement-area planning criticized for adopting urban residential district patterns without sufficient ecological planning, weak landscape integration, and poor adaptation to local terrain [5].

---

**Narrative Summary**

The Massive Southern Shaanxi Migration Program (MSSMP) is one of the largest government-organized resettlement programs in Chinese history, aiming to relocate 2.4 million people from disaster-prone, ecologically fragile, and impoverished mountain communities in southern Shaanxi Province by 2020 [1][2]. The program was launched in 2011 by the Shaanxi Provincial Government in a context of frequent floods, flood-induced landslides, drought, severe soil erosion, and persistent rural poverty. The authors of the reviewed sources frame the MSSMP as a climate-change adaptation strategy, noting observed increases in disaster frequency in recent decades [1][3]. The program is also explicitly tied to the ecological mandate to protect the Han River watershed as a water source for North China's South-to-North Water Transfer Project [2].

Under the MSSMP, eligible households — those in disaster-prone areas, remote areas with poor infrastructure, ecologically sensitive zones, or near water source protection areas — may voluntarily register to move to new resettlement communities, in most cases within their original township boundaries [1][2]. Subsidies ranging from 10,000 to 40,000 yuan are provided for centralized resettlement, and 30,000 yuan for dispersed resettlement, though these cover only a fraction of actual relocation costs, leaving most families reliant on loans from banks, relatives, and friends [1][4]. Village cadres organize village-group meetings to inform eligible households of program rules, compensation levels, and site options; households then register voluntarily [1]. Governments at all levels — provincial, municipal, county, and township — coordinate different stages of implementation, from policy formulation to site approval, construction oversight, and subsidy disbursement [1].

The program has achieved measurable improvements in living conditions and poverty reduction for participating households, with better access to public services and non-farm employment opportunities [2][4]. Ecological service assessments project improvements in water quality, sediment retention, and carbon sequestration [2]. Large declines in disaster casualties and economic losses are documented across the program area between 2011 and 2015 [4]. However, researchers consistently identify a significant equity gap: the poorest households are often excluded because of an undisclosed financial eligibility criterion [1][3]. Remaining residents face increasing isolation and, according to qualitative reporting, reduced social support as out-migration accelerates [1]. Newly resettled migrants face debt burdens, scarcity of farmland in receiving communities, livelihood transformation challenges, and social network disruption [1][2][4]. Some resettlement-area planning has been criticized for replicating urban residential forms without adequate ecological planning or landscape integration [5].

text:
Case study: Oakwood Beach Buyout Program (Oakwood Beach, Staten Island, New York, USA)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Oakwood Beach Buyout Program, Staten Island (Fox Beach, Ocean Breeze, and Graham Beach neighbourhoods), New York City, New York, USA.

**Hazard(s):** The primary hazard driving the retreat decision was coastal flooding and storm surge. Oakwood Beach had been subject to storms and flooding for decades, including a severe nor'easter in 1992 [1]. Hurricane Sandy struck on October 29, 2012, generating storm surges of up to fourteen feet on Staten Island, and was the decisive trigger for the buyout [1, 3, 5, 6]. The chronic infilling of coastal marshes over prior decades had intensified the force of the storm surge as it moved inland [1]. Secondary and cascading hazards included sewage contamination — a combined sewer overflow from a neighbouring sewage treatment plant that released wastewater back into the neighbourhood with the storm surge during Sandy [3, 5] — and wildfire, which is mentioned in the sources as a historical hazard affecting the area over decades, though it was not a primary driver of the buyout decision [1]. Sea level rise and increasing storm frequency and intensity are identified as anticipated future risks in the broader policy context [1, 6].

**Type of Retreat:** Voluntary property buyout program, community-initiated and state-administered. Under the New York State Governor's Office of Storm Recovery (GOSR), eligible homeowners sold their properties at pre-storm market value. As a condition of the program, all existing structures were demolished and the land was permanently restricted to open space — no future redevelopment permitted. A separate New York City acquisition program operated in parallel, allowing potential redevelopment of purchased properties; many Oakwood Beach residents preferred the state program because it prohibited redevelopment and preserved the land as open space [1, 3, 5, 6].

**Scale:** Approximately 321 homes were included in the Oakwood Beach buyout zone [1, 3]. Of the initial Oakwood Beach community, 180 out of 184 homeowners were approved for the buyout [4]. The state had closed on approximately 300 of those Oakwood Beach properties as of April 2017 [3]. The program was subsequently extended to Ocean Breeze (November 2013) and Graham Beach (April 2014) [1, 6]. As of 2019, over 500 properties had been purchased across the three Staten Island buyout communities, and 478 had been returned to nature [1]. By March 2015, there were 500 properties in the enhanced buyout program statewide and approximately 700 more in the separate acquisition program [6].

**Key Actors:** The Oakwood Beach Buyout Committee (community-initiated, grassroots); Governor Andrew Cuomo and the Governor's Office of Storm Recovery (GOSR), the state agency created post-Sandy to coordinate recovery; the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD); FEMA and the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP); the Community Development Block Grant–Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) program; New York City's Build It Back program (a parallel, competing initiative); ProSource Technologies, a Minnesota-based private firm contracted by the state to run the program [5]; planned rewilding of properties was described as involving the Army Corps of Engineers [1]; and the NYC Department of Environmental Protection's Bluebelt programme [1].

**Timeline:**
- October 29, 2012: Hurricane Sandy strikes Staten Island; three residents of Oakwood Beach among 53 deaths on the island; nearly 100 homes destroyed [1].
- Late 2012: Both New York City and New York State announce separate buyout/acquisition programs [1, 3, 5, 6].
- Early 2013: Resident Joseph Tirone raises the buyout idea at a community meeting; the Oakwood Beach Buyout Committee forms and begins canvassing; the Committee approaches Governor Cuomo directly [1, 3, 5].
- April 26, 2013: Federal approval of New York State's CDBG-DR disaster recovery plan [3].
- October–November 2013: First homes purchased just before the one-year anniversary of Sandy; first demolitions begin in November 2013 [1, 3, 5, 6].
- November 2013: Governor Cuomo extends the buyout program to Ocean Breeze [1].
- April 2014: Program extended to Graham Beach; program subsequently closed to additional Staten Island communities [1, 6].
- September 2017: NYC rezones residential areas near state-purchased homes in Oakwood Beach to minimize future development risk [1, 4].
- By 2019: Over 500 properties purchased across the three Staten Island communities; 478 returned to nature [1].
- 2021: Some lots transferred from New York State to New York City government [4].
- 2023: Some of those lots subsequently sold to unidentified private entities [4].
- 2024–2025: A 2025 opinion case study reported that views on the program's long-term success had diverged sharply — while experts lauded short-term outcomes, community members who participated in the Buyout Committee expressed disappointment at mixed-use outcomes that deprioritized ecosystem restoration, including the construction of soccer fields with concrete foundations and the sale of some parcels to private entities [4].

**Key Outcomes:**
- Near-universal (almost 100%) participation rate in Oakwood Beach, widely cited as a critical factor in the program's viability [1].
- Rapid implementation relative to comparable programs: first homes purchased just before the one-year anniversary of Sandy, while the city's Build It Back program had not yet distributed any funds at that point [1].
- Properties were intended to return to marsh/wetland and be integrated into the NYC DEP Bluebelt stormwater management programme; planned rewilding with native grasses and berms by the Army Corps of Engineers was described in the sources [1]. However, later outcomes were mixed [4].
- Significant unresolved issues: unclear and shifting eligibility boundaries; inadequate communication and transparency throughout; financial hardship for some participants due to the "duplication of benefits" deduction; compensation levels insufficient for many to purchase comparable housing in lower-risk areas; and many participants reported that the buyout felt less than fully voluntary in retrospect [3, 5].
- Deep community disappointment at post-buyout land management: some parcels used for soccer fields with concrete foundations [4]; some lots transferred to private entities in 2023 [4]; no long-term environmental management plan was located by the authors of the 2025 case study [4].

---

**Narrative Summary**

Before Hurricane Sandy struck in October 2012, Oakwood Beach was already a community accustomed to flooding. Decades of recurring flood events — including a destructive 1992 nor'easter — had eroded residents' trust in government, reinforced by Staten Island's self-image as New York City's "forgotten borough" [1]. A flood protection berm promised after 1992 took almost a decade to construct and was completely destroyed by Sandy [1]. When Sandy generated a fourteen-foot storm surge, destroyed nearly 100 homes, killed three local residents, and left most of the area without electricity or heat for weeks, many Oakwood Beach residents concluded that rebuilding in place was neither safe nor viable [1]. Rather than waiting passively for the city's recovery program, a local resident named Joseph Tirone proposed the idea of a community buyout at a neighbourhood meeting; the unexpected enthusiasm led to the formation of the Oakwood Beach Buyout Committee, which canvassed door-to-door and approached Governor Cuomo directly [1, 3, 5]. What followed became one of the first large-scale community-initiated managed retreats in the United States [1, 4].

The New York State government responded by leveraging federal HMGP and CDBG-DR funds to purchase homes at pre-storm market value, with all structures demolished and land permanently restricted from future redevelopment. Many residents preferred the state program over the city's competing acquisition plan in part because the state program prohibited redevelopment and preserved the land as open space — they did not want the neighbourhood converted to luxury apartments [1, 3, 5, 6]. Near-universal participation in Oakwood Beach made it a pilot that was subsequently extended to Ocean Breeze and Graham Beach. The first home was purchased just before the one-year anniversary of Sandy, in stark contrast to the city's Build It Back program, which had not yet distributed any funds at that point [1]. By 2019, over 500 properties had been purchased across the three Staten Island communities and 478 had been returned to nature [1].

Yet the picture of success is considerably more complex on closer examination. Many residents described the buyout process as frustrating, confusing, and emotionally difficult: eligibility zone boundaries shifted over time and were never clearly explained; communication from government officials was inconsistent and sometimes contradictory; and compensation, though set at pre-storm market value, was in many cases insufficient to purchase comparable housing in lower-risk areas of the expensive New York City housing market [3, 5]. Federal "duplication of benefits" rules meant that insurance payouts and disaster assistance received by homeowners while waiting for the buyout were later subtracted from the final offer, leaving many with fewer resources for relocation [3, 5]. A substantial share of participants, reflecting three-and-a-half years after the storm, reported that the buyout had come to feel less than truly voluntary — a foregone conclusion shaped by neighbourhood abandonment, fears of eminent domain, and the prospect of rising flood insurance premiums making staying a practical impossibility [3, 5]. A decade on, some community members who championed the retreat have expressed deep disappointment: some parcels have been used for recreational soccer fields with concrete foundations rather than ecological restoration [4], and some lots were sold to unidentified private entities in 2023 — raising concerns about the long-term integrity of the open-space commitments that motivated the original buyout [4].

text:
Case study: Metro Manila Resettlement (Oplan LIKAS) (Metro Manila, Philippines)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case study title:** Monitoring and Evaluation Framework for Resettlement of Coastal Communities in Metro Manila, Philippines.

**Location:** Metro Manila / National Capital Region, Philippines, especially informal settlements along waterways, floodways, rivers, and coastal areas such as Manila Bay.

**Hazard(s):** The sources point to **multiple hazards**, led by **coastal flooding/erosion**, **riverine/pluvial flooding**, and **typhoon impacts**. The thesis also mentions **sea-level rise** as a longer-term exposure factor and notes **fire risk** as part of informal-settlement vulnerability, but flooding and storm-related hazards are the dominant concerns.

**Type of retreat:** The case concerns **planned resettlement/relocation** of informal settler families from hazardous areas. It is a broad policy and planning context rather than a single property buyout or infrastructure realignment project.

**Scale:** The thesis states that **over 104,000 informal settler families**, or about **520,000 people**, live in dangerous areas in Metro Manila. The scope is **metro-regional**, spanning multiple local government units and resettlement sites in or near the metropolis.

**Key actors:** The process is described as **government-led**, especially by the Philippine state and **local government units (LGUs)**. The thesis also emphasizes the roles of affected communities, receiving communities, planners, and implementing institutions in consultation, monitoring, and evaluation. However, the reviewed sources do not document a single implemented project with a clearly identified governance team.

**Timeline:** The thesis says official resettlement approaches in Metro Manila began in the **early 1960s**. It also describes later waves of relocation linked to highway construction, metro rail, and post-disaster resettlement, with climate change increasingly used as a justification for resettlement. The document itself is a **2021** thesis proposing a monitoring and evaluation framework, so the case is best understood as an **ongoing long-running resettlement context** rather than a completed one-off retreat project.

**Key outcomes:** The main output of the reviewed source is a **monitoring and evaluation framework** for future and ongoing resettlement efforts. The framework is designed to assess livelihood assets, settlement conditions, process/institutional quality, and environmental impacts. The thesis argues that successful resettlement should reduce hazard exposure, improve housing and livelihood conditions, preserve social networks, and avoid new forms of impoverishment. At the same time, it highlights recurring problems in Metro Manila resettlement, including weak consultation, resistance to relocation, livelihood disruption, and risks of social and economic harm if relocation is poorly managed.

**Narrative summary:**  
Metro Manila contains many informal settlements in flood-prone and coastal locations. Households in these areas face recurring typhoons, flooding, poor infrastructure, insecure tenure, and limited access to basic services. The thesis treats planned resettlement as a last-resort adaptation option when upgrading or other measures are not enough to reduce risk. It argues that relocation can improve safety, but only if it is carefully planned and monitored.

The central argument of the thesis is that resettlement is not successful simply because people are moved out of danger. Outcomes depend on whether households can maintain livelihoods, whether new settlements are suitable, whether institutions are transparent and coordinated, and whether affected people are meaningfully involved. The framework therefore proposes indicators and methods for tracking both short-term and long-term results, including household surveys, visual inspection, expert interviews, and environmental assessment.

In practical terms, the case shows a long-running Philippine urban resettlement context shaped by flood risk, climate vulnerability, and informal settlement growth. The source documents do not describe one discrete finished retreat project; instead, they document a policy and evaluation framework for improving how resettlement is done. The overall lesson is that managed retreat can reduce exposure, but only if planners also protect livelihoods, social cohesion, service access, and community trust.

Case study: Matata Managed Retreat (Matata, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case name and location:** Awatarariki Fanhead Voluntary Managed Retreat, Matatā, Bay of Plenty, North Island, New Zealand.

**Hazard(s):** Debris flow / landslide, triggered by extreme rainfall in the Awatarariki stream catchment. The managed retreat decision was driven specifically by this debris flow risk. Separately, Matatā as a community is exposed to a broader range of natural hazards — including earthquakes, landslides, floods, coastal erosion and inundation, and far-sourced hazards such as tsunami and volcanic eruption from the Taupō Volcanic Zone — but these broader hazards did not drive the specific managed retreat decision at Awatarariki fanhead [2].

**Type of retreat:** Voluntary property buyout (land acquisition package) offered to individual property owners in the high-risk zone (HRZ), developed using general competency powers under the Local Government Act 2002 s12(2)(a) rather than the Public Works Act 1981. The buyout was supported by two regulatory plan changes: a District Plan Change proposed to rezone the land from Residential to Coastal Protection Zone; and a Regional Plan Change (Bay of Plenty Regional Natural Resources Plan, Plan Change 17) proposed to extinguish existing use rights in the HRZ [2, 3].

**Scale:** The Awatarariki fanhead area contained 45 properties (sections and developed sites), 34 in private ownership, with 16 homes permanently occupied and 18 vacant sections [2]. Matatā's total population was approximately 645 (2013 census); however, the retreat targeted the fanhead properties specifically, not the whole town [2].

**Key actors:** Whakatāne District Council (WDC) — primary implementation body; Bay of Plenty Regional Council (BOPRC) — regional regulatory authority; Central Government (Ministry of Civil Defence and Emergency Management and other agencies) — funding contributor; Tonkin and Taylor (T&T) — specialist engineering consultants; Stimpson & Co. — workshop facilitators; The Property Group Ltd — land acquisition advisors; GNS Science — technical risk research; affected property owners; iwi (Ngāti Rangitihi, Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Tūwharetoa ki Kawerau, and the Mataatua District Māori Council) [2].

**Timeline:** The triggering debris flow occurred in May 2005. Engineering mitigation was pursued from 2005; by December 2012, WDC concluded no viable engineering solutions remained, after which managed retreat was developed over several years. A Consensus Development Group (CDG) was convened March–May 2015. Preliminary buyout offers were made in December 2016. Plan Change 17 was publicly notified in June 2018. Regional and central government agreed to co-fund the buyout in 2019 [2, 3]. The process spans at least 14 years (2005–2019).

**Key outcomes:** By February 2017, 23 landowners had provided registrations of interest: 21 in support of continuing, 2 declining, and 11 non-responses [2]. In 2019, regional and central government agreed to co-fund the buyout through a tripartite model (central government, BOPRC, and WDC each contributing approximately one-third) [3]. Regulatory plan changes were publicly notified and progressed. The case contributed to policy learning on collaborative funding models and risk-based approaches to managed retreat in New Zealand, and the Department of Internal Affairs worked with WDC staff to develop a managed retreat affordability principles framework [2]. The case is also a cautionary example: the protracted timeline, cascading institutional uncertainties, erosion of community trust, and significant and ongoing trauma to residents are extensively documented [2, 3].

---

### Narrative Summary

In May 2005, a severe rainstorm triggered catastrophic debris flows in the Awatarariki stream catchment near the small coastal township of Matatā in the Bay of Plenty, New Zealand. Rocks up to seven metres in diameter were transported at 15–30 km/hr, releasing an estimated 300,000+ cubic metres of rock, wood debris, silt, and slurry onto fanhead properties [2]. The debris flow destroyed 27 homes and damaged a further 87 properties [3]. No lives were lost, although risk assessment modelling later estimated that a repeat event of the same scale could cause five fatalities [2].

In the immediate aftermath, both the community and WDC focused on recovery and selected a debris dam engineering solution. Over the following seven years, engineering designs were repeatedly revised as peer reviews raised concerns about the unprecedented scale, viability, and mounting costs — eventually estimated at $5–7 million or more. By December 2012, WDC concluded no viable engineering solutions remained, after which managed retreat was developed over several further years [2]. Between 2013 and 2016, risk assessments confirmed an intolerable level of loss-of-life risk; a CDG was formed and conducted four full-day workshops considering eight options; cost-benefit and multi-criteria analyses were conducted; and a voluntary acquisition package was developed. The preferred option (Option 2) was costed at between $12.2 million and $14.2 million to acquire 75–100% of the 16 properties with dwellings, the 18 vacant sections, and to cover reserve development costs [2]. Preliminary indicative buyout offers based on current market value were made in December 2016. In parallel, WDC and BOPRC progressed plan changes, creating a perception among many residents that the buyout was not truly voluntary and contributing to mistrust [2, 3]. Residents reported sustained trauma, stress, financial anxiety, and a sense of being trapped. Some residents reported ongoing trauma 13–14 years after the original event; one participant stated they had post-traumatic stress disorder [3]. Funding was agreed in 2019 through a tripartite co-funding model [3].

The Matatā case is instructive at multiple levels. It demonstrates the long-term human costs of short-term post-disaster decision-making, the institutional gaps in New Zealand's managed retreat governance framework, the challenges of implementing voluntary retreat without national policy guidance and confirmed funding, and the cascading nature of uncertainties — technical, financial, legal, political, and social — that compound and reinforce each other. Māori cultural concerns were also significant: the Awatarariki fanhead contains a historically significant burial ground (urupā) whose disturbance had been opposed by local iwi before original development was permitted. The case contributed to New Zealand policy learning on managed retreat and prompted development of national managed retreat affordability principles [2].

Case study: Pointe-Gatineau Home Buyout Program (Pointe-Gatineau, Quebec, Canada)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Pointe Gatineau Managed Retreat / Quebec Provincial Property Buyout Program — Pointe Gatineau, a municipal electoral district within the City of Gatineau, Quebec, Canada [Source 1, Source 3]. Gatineau is located in the Outaouais region of Quebec at the confluence of the Gatineau and Ottawa Rivers, bordering Ontario and the National Capital Region [Sources 2, 3].

**Hazard(s):** Riverine flooding caused by springtime snowmelt and heavy rainfall in the Ottawa River watershed. Pointe Gatineau has a documented flood history spanning more than 200 years, and portions of the community sit within a 1:20-year floodplain (5% annual exceedance probability) [Source 2]. Major flood events occurred in April 2017 and May 2019; the reviewed literature describes these as record-setting floods and, in some places, as approximately 100-year floods [Sources 2, 3].

**Type of Retreat:** Government-sponsored voluntary property buyouts with significant coercive elements, implemented at the individual household level but geographically concentrated in the Pointe Gatineau district. The buyouts were embedded in Quebec's General Indemnity and Financial Assistance Program Regarding Actual or Imminent Disasters (Flooding) and were accompanied by regulatory tools — including the Special Intervention Zone (ZIS) — that prohibited reconstruction in the 0–20-year floodplain, creating strong coercive pressure for properties in that zone and effectively requiring retreat rather than rebuilding [Sources 1, 2, 3].

**Scale:** Approximately 1,800 homes were affected by flooding across the wider City of Gatineau in the 2017 floods [Source 2]. In 2019, 923 properties were damaged in Pointe Gatineau alone [Source 3]. Province-wide disaster claims and buyouts are summarised in Source 1 Table 1: after the 2017 floods, 3,945 homeowners made provincial claims, resulting in 419 buyouts, of which 126 were in Gatineau; after the 2019 floods, 4,964 homeowner claims resulted in 979 buyouts, of which 45 were in Gatineau. After limited 2023 flooding, 797 homeowner claims resulted in 11 provincial buyouts, none in Gatineau [Source 1]. Three years into the process, 185 properties in Pointe Gatineau had been demolished, of which 148 had been officially transferred to the City of Gatineau, with remaining plots still in transfer at the time of reporting [Source 3]. The reviewed sources document no buyouts for tenants in any program cycle, though tenants were eligible for disaster financial assistance [Source 1, Table 1; Source 3].

**Key Actors:** The Government of Quebec (Ministry of Public Security / Directorate General for Recovery) designed and funded the buyout program [Sources 1, 3]. The City of Gatineau handled local implementation, including identifying properties, assessing damage, processing applications, receiving title transfers, and managing demolitions [Source 3]. Community organisations (CREDDO, Park People), design consultants (Mandaworks), and city councillors contributed to post-buyout land use planning [Sources 1, 2]. The federal government played no direct role in the buyout program itself [Sources 2, 3].

**Timeline:**
- **April–May 2017:** Major spring flooding; ad hoc buyout program introduced under the existing disaster financial assistance framework; 126 Gatineau homeowners and 56 Gatineau businesses received buyouts from this cycle [Source 1, Table 1].
- **April–May 2019:** Second major flood, exceeding 2017 levels; Province announced a revised and expanded buyout program. 45 homeowner buyouts and 27 business buyouts in Gatineau from this cycle [Source 1, Table 1].
- **June 2019:** Special Intervention Zone (ZIS) formally enacted; moratorium on construction/reconstruction in 0–20-year floodplain [Sources 1, 3].
- **2019–2021:** 185 properties demolished; 148 officially transferred to the City [Source 3].
- **2020:** Territorial Protection Plan against Floods (PPTFI) introduced with $479 million budget [Source 1]. City of Gatineau city council allocated $1.4 million for post-buyout revitalisation [Sources 2, 3].
- **2020–2021:** City of Gatineau, CREDDO, Park People, and Mandaworks develop the Master Plan (PDA) for vacant lots in Pointe Gatineau and Lac-Beauchamp districts [Source 1].
- **March 2022:** ZIS replaced by the Transitional Regime for the Management of Flood Zones, Banks and Coastlines (TRMFZBC), which lifted the ZIS and empowered municipalities to authorise development in flood zones, though in practice it imposed additional procedural requirements and costs [Source 1].
- **July 2022:** Compensation caps raised to $325,000 (residence) and $60,000 (land); small businesses eligible for up to $485,000 [Source 1].
- **2023:** Minor flooding; 11 provincial buyouts, none in Gatineau [Source 1].
- **2024:** Province planning new flood maps and regulatory framework (OPI); Master Plan (PDA) funded but largely unimplemented; Gatineau described as "partially retreated" [Source 1].

**Key Outcomes:**
- 185 properties demolished and 148 officially transferred to municipal ownership in Pointe Gatineau, creating a "swiss-cheese" or checkerboard landscape [Sources 1, 2, 3].
- The province achieved partial alignment between buyout programs and regulatory tools (ZIS, then TRMFZBC), restricting rebuilding in high-risk zones — though the policy environment also exhibited significant fragmentation [Source 1].
- A community Master Plan (PDA) for vacant lots was developed but remains largely unimplemented due to funding gaps and absence of provincial direction on updated flood maps [Source 1].
- A municipal official stated that the tax base had been cut by "probably 30%," creating ongoing service delivery challenges [Source 1].
- Significant bureaucratic delays and lack of intergovernmental coordination were widely criticised [Sources 1, 2, 3].
- The reviewed sources report little or no dedicated relocation assistance — including no help for bought-out homeowners in finding safer housing [Sources 1, 2].
- Tenants were eligible for disaster financial assistance but the reviewed sources document no tenants receiving buyouts in any program cycle [Source 1, Table 1].

---

**Narrative Summary**

Pointe Gatineau is a working-class riverine neighbourhood in the City of Gatineau, Quebec, located at the confluence of the Gatineau and Ottawa Rivers [Sources 2, 3]. It has a documented flood history stretching back more than 200 years [Source 2]. After two successive and record-breaking spring flood events in April 2017 and May 2019 — described in the literature as approximately 100-year floods — the Province of Quebec introduced and then expanded a government-sponsored property buyout program enabling homeowners to permanently vacate flood-damaged properties in exchange for financial compensation [Sources 1, 2, 3]. The buyouts were framed as voluntary, but the simultaneous introduction of lifetime limits on disaster assistance and prohibitions on reconstruction in the 0–20-year floodplain created strong coercive pressure on homeowners — and, for those in the ZIS zone, effectively required retreat rather than rebuilding [Sources 1, 3]. Three years after the 2019 floods, 185 properties in Pointe Gatineau had been demolished, of which 148 had been officially transferred to the City of Gatineau [Source 3].

The experience in Pointe Gatineau illustrates both the potential and the limitations of managed retreat implemented reactively in a post-disaster environment. On the positive side, the province partially aligned buyout policy with regulatory tools (the ZIS, and subsequently the TRMFZBC) to restrict rebuilding in high-risk zones, representing a notable evolution in Canadian flood risk governance [Source 1]. On the negative side, the buyout process was widely criticised for excessive bureaucracy, lengthy application delays, insufficient compensation for some homeowners, narrow eligibility criteria, and a near-total absence of support for homeowners in finding alternative housing. Tenants — who filed hundreds of disaster claims — received no buyouts under any program cycle [Source 1, Table 1].

Five years after the 2019 floods, Pointe Gatineau remains in what Source 1 describes as a "partially retreated" state. The vacant lots created by the buyouts present an opportunity for ecological restoration and community revitalisation. The City of Gatineau, with partners including CREDDO, Park People, and Mandaworks, developed an ambitious Master Plan (PDA) proposing nature lots, nourishing lots, gathering lots, by-the-shore lots, and sponge lots [Source 1]. However, as of early 2024, this plan has not been fully implemented, largely because the Province has not released updated flood maps needed to confirm permissible land uses, and adequate funding and administrative guidance from the province remain absent [Source 1]. The case illustrates a recurring governance challenge: the entity with the financial resources to fund buyouts (the provincial government) has limited involvement in the post-buyout phase, while the entity responsible for managing the land (the municipality) lacks the resources and guidance to act [Source 1].

Case study: Hambantota Post-Tsunami Relocation (Hambantota, Sri Lanka)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

### Case Name and Location

Post-Tsunami Community Resettlement in Sri Lanka, with primary case material drawn from the Siribopura Resettlement Housing Program in Hambantota District, and supplementary coverage of resettlement sites in Ampara, Galle (Akmeemana), and Matara Districts. Sri Lanka, South Asia (Global South).

### Hazard(s)

The primary hazard driving relocation was the Indian Ocean Tsunami of 26 December 2004, a catastrophic coastal event. The tsunami affected nearly 65% of Sri Lanka's coastline (about 1,000 km), killed over 30,000 people, and displaced more than 500,000 people [1, 2]. Destruction of housing was the largest single category of physical damage [2].

### Type of Retreat

The retreat took the form of a mandatory, government-directed community resettlement away from a declared coastal buffer zone (initially 100–200 m, later revised to 55–100 m). Displaced households within the buffer zone were relocated to donor-built permanent housing in new inland settlement sites under a "donor-driven" model. An alternative "Owner-Driven Reconstruction" (ODR) program allowed households outside the buffer zone to rebuild in place with financial assistance.

### Scale

Initial estimates suggested approximately 50,000 families would need relocation; following policy revision after the November 2005 election, the no-building zone was reduced from 100–200 m to 55–100 m, lowering the estimated relocation requirement to approximately 30,000 households [1]. This translated to 29,830 housing units in relocated sites across affected districts [1]. By the middle of 2005, THRU had finalised plans to build 485 housing projects in 11 districts [2]. In Hambantota District, the Siribopura site accommodated 1,083 tsunami-affected households, along with others displaced for different reasons [3, 6]. Across the country, approximately 4,643 units were required in Hambantota's relocation sites (against a housing requirement of only 1,057 per initial TAFREN estimates), while Ampara required approximately 3,721 units [1].

### Key Actors

- **Government of Sri Lanka (GoSL)**: Set policy, declared buffer zones, established institutional mechanisms, and coordinated land acquisition and beneficiary selection through Divisional Secretariats.
- **Task Force for Rebuilding the Nation (TAFREN)** and **Tsunami Housing Reconstruction Unit (THRU)**: Primary initial coordinating bodies, both dissolved in November 2005 [2].
- **Reconstruction and Development Agency (RADA)**: Successor coordination body, created in November 2005 [1, 2].
- **Urban Development Authority (UDA)**: Responsible for layout preparation, guidelines, and coordination of permanent housing sites.
- **National Housing Development Authority (NHDA)**: Issued housing and planning guidelines.
- **International and domestic donor agencies and NGOs**: Constructed housing under the donor-driven model (Suchi Foundation, Singapore Red Cross, Sajith Foundation, Suboda Foundation, Care International, and others) [6].
- **Ports Authority of Sri Lanka**: Managed compensation for harbour development-related displacement in Hambantota, separate from the tsunami resettlement program [6].
- **University of Moratuwa**: Conducted the 2006 Rapid Environmental Assessment (REA) of 409 housing sites [2].
- **Affected communities**: Had limited and largely nominal involvement in planning; in practice, their preferences were often not reflected in final site allocations [1, 2, 5].

### Timeline

- **26 December 2004**: Tsunami strikes; government declares buffer zones (100–200 m).
- **Early 2005**: TAFREN and THRU established; donor-driven reconstruction begins; buffer zone at 100–200 m.
- **2005–2006**: Owner-driven reconstruction proceeds more rapidly and cost-effectively than donor-driven construction.
- **November 2005**: TAFREN and THRU dissolved; RADA created as successor coordination agency [1, 2].
- **After November 2005 election**: No-building zone revised from 100–200 m to 55–100 m, reducing estimated households requiring relocation to approximately 30,000 [1].
- **2005–2008**: Donor-built housing units progressively completed and handed over (Hambantota ahead of schedule; Ampara severely delayed).
- **2006**: University of Moratuwa REA of 409 sites conducted, though construction was already underway at most sites by that time [2].
- **2007/2008**: Harbour development-induced resettlement in Hambantota; Ports Authority compensation program implemented for 454 households [6].
- **2008–2009**: World Habitat Research Center (WHRC) study of relocation outcomes conducted in Ampara and Hambantota [1].
- **2011**: Primary surveys in Siribopura and Hambantota for land market and success/failure analyses [3, 6].
- **2016**: Household surveys conducted for long-term satisfaction study covering 12 sites in Galle, Matara, and Hambantota [2].
- **Status**: Post-retreat; follow-up studies confirm persistent dissatisfaction and unresolved land tenure issues more than a decade after the event.

### Key Outcomes

Outcomes were mixed and varied significantly by district and site. Hambantota benefited from disproportionate donor interest and political attention, as it was the native district of Sri Lanka's president at the time of the tsunami [1]. This resulted in far more housing being built than was required by tsunami-affected households; many units were distributed to non-tsunami-affected households through political patronage [1]. Ampara's reconstruction was severely delayed and constrained by ethnic conflict and LTTE activity [1, 4].

Physical housing quality varied substantially by district and site: Hambantota houses were generally assessed as satisfactory, while Ampara included several sites with poor construction and inadequate infrastructure [1]. Across all three southern districts studied by Manatunge et al. [2], construction defects, inappropriate designs, poor ventilation, and inadequate infrastructure were common.

Land tenure remained unresolved for the majority of resettlers for years after occupancy. In the Hambantota Siribopura sites, as of 2011, only 38 of the 1,083 tsunami-affected resettled households had received formal title deeds (free grants), while the majority possessed only informal letters from donor agencies [3]. This created informal land markets, barriers to credit, and ongoing tenure insecurity.

Livelihood disruption was severe, particularly for fishing communities relocated far from the coast. Women's livelihoods were disproportionately disrupted [1]. Community participation in planning was limited to nominal or token processes at best, and was identified across multiple sources as a primary cause of dissatisfaction [2, 5]. Long-term satisfaction surveys more than a decade after the tsunami confirmed widespread dissatisfaction across most sites [2].

### Narrative Summary

On 26 December 2004, the Indian Ocean Tsunami devastated Sri Lanka's coastline, killing over 30,000 people and displacing more than 500,000. The government's immediate response was to declare coastal buffer zones (initially 100–200 m from the sea) where no reconstruction would be permitted, requiring the relocation of approximately 50,000 households. This policy was announced in a context of "profound emotion" [1], without pre-existing legal or institutional frameworks for disaster-induced resettlement, and under enormous pressure from international donors and political actors to move quickly. There were no pre-existing policy frameworks or institutional arrangements readily available for post-tsunami resettlement [2]. Following a change in government in November 2005, the buffer zone was reduced to 55–100 m, reducing the relocation requirement to approximately 30,000 households. The scale of international aid flowing into the country was unprecedented, but so were the coordination failures.

For those within the buffer zone, the government and a large array of international and domestic NGOs constructed new housing in inland resettlement sites—a "donor-driven" model in which houses were planned and built by external agencies and then allocated to beneficiaries. Affected communities had limited and largely nominal involvement in planning; in practice, their preferences were often not reflected in final site allocations [1, 5]. People from different villages were placed in the same new settlements, breaking social networks. Sites were frequently located in unsuitable terrain—waterlogged, hilly, or remote—far from original livelihoods, especially fishing harbours and markets [1, 2]. Physical construction quality was often problematic, with cracked walls, collapsed roofs, inadequate ventilation and sanitation, and absent common spaces in many sites [2]. Most resettlers did not receive formal legal title to their land for years, leaving them unable to access formal credit and vulnerable to informal land market exploitation [3, 6].

Outcomes varied sharply by district. Hambantota received more housing than it needed, with political interference channelling units to non-tsunami-affected households. Ampara, affected by both the tsunami and civil conflict, saw severe reconstruction delays, with housing inequitably distributed across ethnic lines. For resettlers across the studied districts, incomes generally declined, expenditures rose, and women's livelihoods were particularly disrupted [1]. Studies conducted more than a decade later confirm that many resettlers remain dissatisfied, houses have been abandoned or sold informally, and the social and economic rehabilitation promised at the outset has largely not been achieved [2, 3, 6]. The case stands as a cautionary example of reactive, top-down, politically influenced disaster resettlement conducted without adequate community participation, planning, or attention to livelihood sustainability.

Case study: Cedar Rapids Buyout Program (Cedar Rapids, Iowa, USA)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Cedar Rapids Voluntary Property Acquisition Program, Cedar Rapids, Iowa, United States (Linn County)

**Hazard(s):** Riverine flooding from the Cedar River. The 2008 flood was the primary triggering disaster event. The Cedar River crested at 31.1 feet on June 13, 2008 — surpassing the previous record of 20 feet — and inundated over 10 square miles of the city [1][2]. Source [1] documents major historical Cedar River floods in 1929, 1961, 1965, 1993, and 2008. Source [3] documents 26 flood disasters since 1980 and droughts in 1988, 2003, and 2012 in the broader Middle Cedar River basin, along with water quality concerns from agricultural nutrient runoff. The property acquisition program was driven specifically by riverine flood risk from the 2008 event.

**Type of Retreat:** Voluntary individual property buyout program, embedded within a broader post-flood recovery and flood risk management strategy that combined levees, removable floodwalls, green space, and neighbourhood revitalization [1].

**Scale:** The program acquired 1,356 flood-damaged properties at a total cost of approximately $93.9 million, closing on June 30, 2014 [1]. The 2008 flood displaced more than 18,000 residents and affected 5,390 homes [1][2]. The acquisitions were concentrated along the Cedar River floodplain and organized into three management areas spanning both sides of the river [1].

**Key Actors:** The City of Cedar Rapids was the primary implementing authority. Federal funding came from FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) program, including a special Congressional appropriation of $300 million for 2008 Midwest floods [1]. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), Rock Island District (MVR), played a key role in the complementary Flood Control System (FCS) design and risk assessment [2]. Local funding was supplemented by a Local Option Sales Tax (LOST) approved by Cedar Rapids voters in 2009, generating revenues used as cost-match for buyouts and flood mitigation [4]. The State of Iowa Flood Mitigation Board was established in 2013 at Cedar Rapids' proposal to the state legislature, and gave its first award to Cedar Rapids [5]. Multiple community organizations, nonprofits, and government agencies participated in recovery programming [5].

**Timeline:**
- June 13, 2008: Historic flooding event; Cedar River crests at 31.1 feet [1][2]
- 2008 (within days of flood): City Council convened recovery planning process; 10-month public participation process began involving more than 2,600 community members [5]
- 2008–2009: River Corridor Redevelopment Plan developed; Voluntary Acquisition Program launched [1]
- 2009: Local Option Sales Tax established to supplement federal buyout funding [4]
- 2010: USACE feasibility study finalized (November 2010); Chief of Engineers Report signed January 2011 [2]
- 2011: MVR tasked ERDC-CHL with risk assessment of removable floodwalls on the eastern side of the Cedar River [2]
- 2013: State of Iowa Flood Mitigation Board established; first award given to Cedar Rapids [5]
- June 30, 2014: Voluntary Acquisition Program closed; 1,356 properties acquired for $93.9 million [1]
- 2016: ERDC-CHL scope expanded to include both sides of the Cedar River; Phase 1 study initiated [2]
- March 2019: Phase 2 of the risk assessment initiated [2]
- September 2016: Multi-Hazard Tournament (MHT) conducted in Cedar Rapids involving 36 stakeholders from the Cedar River basin [3]
- March 2020: ERDC/USACE final risk assessment report published [2]

**Key Outcomes:** The program successfully acquired 1,356 flood-affected properties for $93.9 million [1]. A parcel-level benefit-cost analysis found the acquisitions cost-effective, with 88% of Greenway Area parcels and 88% of Construction Area parcels passing a BCR > 1.0 test; only 46% of Neighbourhood Revitalization Area parcels passed, consistent with that area's primary recovery (not mitigation) mission [1]. The acquired lands were repurposed across three management zones: a Greenway Area (parks, trails, ecological benefits), a Construction Area (site of levees and floodwalls), and a Neighbourhood Revitalization Area (affordable replacement housing) [1]. Social equity analysis found a moderately strong positive association between socially vulnerable neighbourhoods and buyout resources (Spearman r = 0.657, p < 0.01), though where displaced residents ultimately relocated remains unclear [1]. The complementary FCS risk assessment work was ongoing, with ERDC's final report on removable floodwall deployment risks published in March 2020 [2].

---

**Narrative Summary**

In June 2008, the Cedar River crested at a historic 31.1 feet in Cedar Rapids, Iowa — over 11 feet above the previous record of 20 feet — inundating more than 10 square miles and 1,300 city blocks, flooding 5,390 homes, displacing approximately 18,000 residents, and generating over $3 billion in economic losses [1]. With over $5.4 billion in total damages to Cedar Rapids [5], the flood was a defining catastrophe for the community. Within four days, city government began mobilizing a recovery response, and over the following ten months, a broad public participation process — involving more than 2,600 community members — produced the River Corridor Redevelopment Plan and a preferred flood management strategy [5].

A key element of that plan was the Voluntary Property Acquisition Program, which used federal HMGP and CDBG funds — augmented by a locally approved sales tax — to purchase 1,356 flood-damaged properties over six years (2008–2014) for a total of $93.9 million [1][4]. Property owners were offered 107% of their pre-flood assessed value, adjusted downward where duplication of benefits existed [1]. The acquired parcels were organized into three management zones: a Greenway Area (open space, parks, and ecological benefits along the river, deed-restricted against future development for HMGP-funded properties); a Construction Area (site of new levees and floodwalls); and a Neighbourhood Revitalization Area (affordable replacement housing for buyers with incomes below the area median) [1]. A parcel-level benefit-cost analysis confirmed that acquisitions were economically justified for flood-risk properties, and a social vulnerability analysis found that buyout resources were moderately and positively aligned with socially vulnerable neighbourhoods — though the fate of displaced residents remains incompletely documented [1].

Alongside the buyout program, Cedar Rapids pursued a complementary structural Flood Control System consisting of levees, earthen berms, and a network of removable floodwalls and gates along both banks of the Cedar River. ERDC-CHL conducted multi-phase risk assessments of the removable components between 2011 and 2020, using RiskyProject Monte Carlo analysis to evaluate deployment alternatives [2]. In September 2016, a Multi-Hazard Tournament involving 36 stakeholders from the Cedar River basin used the Iowa Watershed Decision Support System (IoWaDSS) to collaboratively explore mitigation strategies for the basin's interconnected flood, drought, and water quality hazards [3]. As of the final ERDC report in March 2020, the city continued to advance its flood risk management infrastructure [2].

text:
Case study: Grand Forks Floodplain Buyout (Grand Forks, North Dakota, USA)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Grand Forks Flood Buyout and Recovery Program, Grand Forks, North Dakota, United States. Grand Forks is located on the western bank of the north-flowing Red River, adjacent to its sister city East Grand Forks, Minnesota [Parry et al. 2020, p. 31].

**Hazard(s):** Riverine flooding from the Red River, with a concurrent cascading electrical fire in the historic business district triggered when floodwaters prevented fire truck access.

**Type of Retreat:** Large-scale voluntary property acquisition and recovery program, funded primarily through federal HMGP and CDBG-DR grants and paired with downtown redevelopment and replacement housing efforts. Over 800 residential and commercial properties were acquired, demolished, and the land converted to permanent open space. A parallel component involved constructing replacement housing for displaced residents and a downtown revitalization effort.

**Scale:** The 1997 Red River flood caused the evacuation of roughly 60,000 residents from Grand Forks and East Grand Forks combined. Grand Forks subsequently purchased over 800 residential and commercial properties across multiple neighbourhoods along the Red River corridor — one of the largest buyout programs in U.S. history at the time.

**Key Actors:** City of Grand Forks; FEMA (HMGP funding); U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (CDBG-DR funding); State of North Dakota (reduced federal cost-share rate); U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (flood protection planning); Grand Forks Homes (non-profit housing developer for replacement housing); Fannie Mae's Housing Impact Fund (replacement housing financing); mayors of Grand Forks and East Grand Forks (political champions who lobbied Congress and President Clinton).

**Timeline:** Triggering flood event: April 1997. Federal disaster declaration and initiation of buyout program: 1997. Buyout acquisitions and demolitions completed approximately 1997–1999. Replacement housing construction: approximately 1998–1999. Riverfront greenway and infrastructure realignment: completed by the early 2000s. By 2018, Grand Forks' population had grown to 70,770 [Parry et al. 2020, p. 35]. The case is post-retreat and is referenced in the academic literature as a completed, if contested, program.

**Key Outcomes:** Acquired riverfront land was converted into approximately 20 miles of paved multi-purpose trails, two golf courses, boat ramps, campgrounds, ice skating rinks, basketball and tennis courts, softball, soccer, and football fields, and more — a celebrated greenway and floodplain buffer [Parry et al. 2020, p. 32]. Critical infrastructure (water treatment plant electrical systems) was relocated above the 1997 flood level, and a new elementary school was built above base-flood elevation; new building codes were implemented before allowing downtown rebuilding. By 2018, Grand Forks city officials reported the downtown was "stronger than it was before the flood" [Parry et al. 2020, p. 35]. However, the program generated significant controversy: residents filed a class-action lawsuit alleging bullying and unfair pricing; duplication-of-benefits rules reduced net payments; the city ultimately used eminent domain for some properties along the dike line; and replacement housing was unaffordable and poorly located, with only 12 of 180 homes selling in the first two years. The city's jobs market has remained "relatively flat over the last two decades, in contrast to neighbouring cities that continue to grow" [Parry et al. 2020, pp. 35–36].

---

**Narrative Summary**

In April 1997, the Red River crested at 54 feet — 26 feet above flood stage — following an exceptionally severe winter of record cold, eight blizzards, and over 100 inches of snowfall across the Red River Valley [Parry et al. 2020, pp. 30–31]. Nearly all of Grand Forks' roughly 60,000 residents (across both Grand Forks and East Grand Forks) were evacuated. Floodwaters submerged or partially submerged close to 300 homes in Grand Forks, triggered a cascading electrical fire that destroyed eleven historic buildings in the business district when flooded roads prevented fire truck access, and damaged 70% of the city's schools [Parry et al. 2020, p. 31]. Total damage was estimated at $3.5 billion [Parry et al. 2020, p. 31]. The disaster was compounded by the fact that many residents lacked flood insurance, having been advised by agents that it was unnecessary based on the National Weather Service's forecast of a 49-foot crest — well below the actual 54-foot event [Parry et al. 2020, pp. 31–32].

In the aftermath, the mayors of Grand Forks and East Grand Forks lobbied Congress and President Clinton directly for recovery funding. The city received approximately $171 million in HUD CDBG-DR funding and an additional $13 million in FEMA HMGP funding, with North Dakota also receiving a reduced federal cost-share rate [Parry et al. 2020, p. 32]. Grand Forks used this funding to purchase over 800 residential and commercial properties. River-side properties were demolished and the land converted into an approximately 20-mile riverfront greenway. Critical infrastructure was rebuilt or relocated above the 1997 flood level, new building codes were implemented, and a new elementary school was constructed above base flood elevation [Parry et al. 2020, pp. 32–35].

Despite being widely referenced as a successful managed retreat, the program was deeply contentious. Buyout managers had preconceived notions about which areas would be acquired but did not communicate this openly to residents [Parry et al. 2020, p. 33]. Federal duplication-of-benefits rules reduced net payments for those who had already received non-profit or insurance assistance. Residents filed a class-action lawsuit alleging bullying and unfair pricing, and the city ultimately resorted to eminent domain for some properties along the dike line [Parry et al. 2020, pp. 33–34; Siders 2019, pp. 249–250]. The replacement housing program — 180 homes built on the undeveloped west edge of the city, priced from $105,000 to $147,000 despite replacing homes valued at $50,000–$80,000 — largely failed to attract displaced residents, with only 12 of 180 homes selling by February 1999 [Parry et al. 2020, p. 35]. The case is frequently cited in the academic literature as an example of buyout program transparency and social equity concerns [Siders 2019, p. 244].
