Case study: Allenville (Allenville, Arizona, United States)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

### Case Name and Location
Allenville, Arizona, United States (relocated to Hopeville, Arizona). Allenville was a small, unincorporated rural community situated near the Gila River in the southwestern United States, in the Buckeye Valley area of Maricopa County.

### Hazard(s)
Recurrent, severe riverine flooding caused by upstream water management releases from reservoirs on the Salt River, Verde River, and Agua Fria River — the three rivers converging into the Gila River approximately 15 miles east of Allenville. Perry & Lindell (1997) explain that major water releases were required during periods of heavy rain and snow-melt on northern Arizona watersheds to avoid the possibility of dam collapse, making repeated seasonal flooding of Allenville essentially inevitable once the water management infrastructure was in place.

### Type of Retreat
This was a community-scale, permanent relocation in which an entire small settlement was collectively moved intact to a newly constructed site (Hopeville) on nearby state land, selected jointly by the community organization and government agencies. The process involved the negotiated sale of Allenville properties and acquisition of the new Hopeville site. No demolition of Allenville structures is explicitly documented in the reviewed sources.

### Scale
At the time of relocation, Allenville was composed of 15 permanent homes and 20 mobile homes — 35 housing units in total [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50]. Twenty-six of these households were interviewed at the new Hopeville site; an additional six households that relocated elsewhere in the Buckeye Valley area were also traced and interviewed [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50]. The community rarely exceeded fifty households [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50]. The community was predominantly Black American, older (more than 20% over the age of 60 and another 30% between 41 and 59), and economically disadvantaged, with a median family income of just above $7,000 per year and approximately one-third of families below the federally established poverty level [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50, citing Arizona Division of Emergency Management, 1979, and Army Corps of Engineers, 1980].

### Key Actors
- **Allenville Citizens for Progress (ACP):** A non-profit community organization formed in 1965 with an elected Board of Directors that served as the primary community representative and negotiating agent throughout the relocation process [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50].
- **Arizona State Division of Emergency Management (Arizona DEM):** Served as the local sponsor of the relocation [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 51].
- **U.S. Army Corps of Engineers:** Conducted a cost study of various structural and non-structural mitigation measures and participated in site selection [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 51].
- **U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA):** Listed among the principal agencies in the multi-organizational relocation context [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 54]; FEMA had also incorporated relocation into its national hazard mitigation strategy [FEMA, 1995, cited in Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 49].
- **Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) — Phoenix office:** Listed among agencies interviewed for the case study and among the principal agencies involved [Perry & Lindell, 1997, pp. 50, 54].
- **Maricopa County Department of Community Development:** Listed among agencies interviewed and among the principal agencies [Perry & Lindell, 1997, pp. 50, 54]. Perry & Lindell's description refers to "a County Office of Community Development."
- **Private businesses:** Also mentioned among actors in the multi-organizational context, though without detail [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 54].

### Timeline
- **1940s:** Allenville established near the Gila River by unskilled agricultural workers [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50].
- **1965:** First flooding along the Gila River to affect Allenville (affecting only a small part of the community); ACP established [Perry & Lindell, 1997, pp. 50–51].
- **March 1978:** A large upstream water release floods the entire community; water marks as high as six feet above ground level; all residents evacuated; extensive property damage; most buildings rendered uninhabitable [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 51].
- **Late 1970s–early 1980s:** Additional major floods; decision to pursue relocation emerges; Army Corps of Engineers conducts a cost study of structural and non-structural alternatives; ACP petitions to establish its formal legal standing to represent the community; site selection and property negotiations begin [Perry & Lindell, 1997, pp. 51–52].
- **Interim period:** A period of more than three years elapsed between residents leaving Allenville and occupying Hopeville; most residents lived in a mobile home park (interim housing) administered by Arizona DEM; a few families were scattered in communities throughout the area [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 52].
- **Completion:** Residents moved into the newly constructed community of Hopeville; "both the relocatees and the agencies involved in the relocation characterized the move in positive, successful terms" [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 53].
- **Post-relocation (retrospective):** Perry & Lindell (1997) conducted their research approximately six months after relocated citizens had moved to Hopeville; the case is described as post-retreat in the reviewed literature.
- **1997:** Perry & Lindell's retrospective case study published, documenting outcomes.

### Key Outcomes
The Allenville-to-Hopeville relocation is frequently cited in the managed retreat literature as a positive example of intact community relocation [Greer & Binder, 2017; Greer et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2025; Cross et al., 2025]. Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 53) report that "virtually all citizens questioned expressed satisfaction with the move," and that both relocatees and agencies characterized the move in positive, successful terms. Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 53) also note that "Hopeville has flourished, slightly increasing population size over the years, although remaining a close-knit, racially and economically homogeneous community." Job opportunities increased following the construction of a nuclear power plant in the region; completion of an interstate highway to California improved access and increased commerce; and a cultural museum was constructed and operated by the community association [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 53]. The primary documented challenges included the lengthy interim waiting period (over three years), anxiety during the interim housing phase, concerns about distance to services, and modest financial uncertainty among lower-income residents. A small number of households (six, from Perry & Lindell's interview sample) relocated outside the planned community site rather than to Hopeville.

**Important caveat:** These post-relocation outcomes are reported by Perry & Lindell (1997) in a retrospective case study conducted approximately six months after residents moved to Hopeville, with longer-term positive observations (nuclear power plant, interstate highway, museum) apparently based on the authors' knowledge at the time of writing rather than systematic longitudinal monitoring. The sources do not report independent verification or formal evaluation of these outcomes.

### Narrative Summary

Allenville was a small, predominantly Black American community established in the early 1940s near the Gila River in Arizona's Buckeye Valley. For decades it remained a close-knit, racially and economically homogeneous rural settlement, rarely exceeding fifty households. Residents were predominantly older and working-class, with many living on fixed retirement incomes, and the community operated under an active non-profit organization — the Allenville Citizens for Progress (ACP) — in the absence of formal municipal incorporation. Beginning in 1965, the construction of upstream water management reservoirs made seasonal flooding of the Gila River increasingly severe. After the catastrophic March 1978 flood, which inundated the entire community and left water marks up to six feet above ground level, both the ACP and Arizona emergency management officials concluded that the town was in an untenable position. ACP investigated whether the upstream water releases could be stopped or whether structural flood protection (levees, channelization) was feasible, ultimately concluding neither option was viable. The decision to pursue permanent relocation emerged jointly from the community and state emergency management during roughly the same period.

The relocation process was organized around ACP's formal recognition as the community's legal bargaining agent — established through a community petition — and implemented through a multi-agency consortium including Arizona DEM (as local sponsor), the Army Corps of Engineers, FEMA, HUD's Phoenix office, and the Maricopa County Department of Community Development. A new community site was selected from nearby state lands through a joint process between ACP and the agencies. Most residents lived in a mobile home park administered by Arizona DEM during the interim period of more than three years between leaving Allenville and occupying Hopeville. Throughout this period, ACP maintained regular communications with residents to minimize rumor and maintain morale, and sought visible support from state and county political figures to reassure relocatees.

The case is frequently cited in the managed retreat literature as a positive example of community-centered relocation, notable for the pre-existing strength of ACP, the community's own framing of the process as an effort to preserve Allenville as a community rather than a displacement imposed from outside, and the maintenance of social networks during the transition. Perry & Lindell (1997) report broad resident satisfaction and describe Hopeville as having flourished in subsequent years. The relocation is now used as a reference point for principles of effective, citizen-centered community relocation across the hazard mitigation and managed retreat literature.

Case study: Portland (Portland, Oregon, United States)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** East Lents Floodplain Restoration Project, Portland, Oregon, United States.

**Hazard(s):** Flooding, including riverine and stormwater-driven (fluvial, pluvial, and infrastructural) flood risk from Johnson Creek, a creek that runs through southeast Portland and is described as a recurring site of flooding.

**Type of Retreat:** Voluntary property buyout program. The City of Portland's Bureau of Environmental Services (BES) administers a "Willing Seller Program" associated with the Johnson Creek Restoration Plan, through which flood-prone residential properties in the East Lents neighborhood are acquired from willing homeowners, structures are demolished, and the land is converted to floodplain open space and ecological restoration areas.

**Scale:** The reviewed sources do not provide a precise count of acquired parcels or displaced households specifically for the East Lents project, nor do they document total funding amounts for this specific project. Lloyd et al. (2026) describe the Portland Johnson Creek Restoration Plan's "Willing Seller Program" as having "the highest number of buyout homes among our study cities" (Portland, Phoenix, Atlanta, and Baltimore), characterizing it as a successful program implemented at "limited scales." No household counts or dollar figures for the East Lents project specifically are available in the reviewed corpus.

**Key Actors:** The City of Portland Bureau of Environmental Services (BES) is the primary administering agency. Lloyd et al. (2026) list multiple agencies involved in Portland flood risk management, including the Portland Bureau of Planning and Sustainability (PBPS), Portland Bureau of Transportation (PBOT), Portland Water Bureau (PWB), Portland Park Bureau (PPB), Multnomah County Drainage District (MCDD), the Oregon Department of Emergency Management (ODEM), and FEMA Region 10, among others (see Appendix A of Lloyd et al., 2026). Federal funding through FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) is identified in the broader Portland program context; Lloyd et al. (2026) also reference "federal and state money" in the context of Baltimore buyout sites, and the general HMGP structure described by Siders (2018) applies to programs of this type.

**Timeline:** The primary source cited in the project's source list is a 2012 City of Portland BES document. However, the full text of this document was not available in the reviewed corpus, so no project-specific start date or milestone chronology can be verified from the reviewed materials. Lloyd et al. (2026) describe Portland's buyout program as ongoing, with practitioners referencing flood events including a recorded peak flow in Johnson Creek in 2015 and the 1996 Oregon flood. The Vanucchi et al. (2025) study notes that exemplary U.S. buyout programs like Austin's began in the 1980s and operate as "standing programs," not solely post-disaster. Whether the broader Portland Johnson Creek program shares this standing-program character is suggested by Lloyd et al.'s (2026) description of BES being "proactive in restoration efforts," but no verified continuous timeline is available from the reviewed sources.

**Key Outcomes:** Outcomes described in the reviewed sources are general and programmatic rather than project-specific for East Lents. Lloyd et al. (2026) cite Portland's Willing Seller Program as an example of success in "negotiating voluntary buyouts" and "restoring floodplains." The intent of the program is to reduce flood exposure, demolish at-risk structures, and convert floodplain land to open space and ecological restoration. Broader literature (Vanucchi et al., 2025; Siders, 2018) notes that buyout programs of this type commonly result in structure demolition and open-space requirements under HMGP, but also that ecological restoration of post-buyout lands is often incomplete, with many parcels remaining as maintained lawns rather than restored floodplain habitats.

---

### Narrative Summary

The East Lents Floodplain Restoration Project is a voluntary property buyout and floodplain restoration effort in the East Lents neighborhood of Portland, Oregon, situated along Johnson Creek in the southeast of the city. Johnson Creek is described by Portland flood risk practitioners as "a site of recurring flooding," and Portland broadly faces "fluvial, pluvial, and infrastructural flood risk" expected to increase in the future (Lloyd et al., 2026). The project is part of Portland's Johnson Creek Restoration Plan and is administered by the City of Portland Bureau of Environmental Services (BES) through a "Willing Seller Program," under which individual homeowners voluntarily sell flood-prone properties to the city. Structures are then demolished and the land is maintained as open space, consistent with FEMA Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) requirements.

Portland practitioners interviewed by Lloyd et al. (2026) described Portland's program as having "the highest number of buyout homes among our study cities" — the four cities studied being Portland, Phoenix, Atlanta, and Baltimore — and cited the Johnson Creek Restoration Plan as a positive example of flood risk mitigation through voluntary buyouts. Practitioners noted that BES has been "proactive in restoration efforts to improve their drainage systems" and referenced the importance of integrating buyouts into a broader planning vision for floodplain restoration. The program has also been noted for connecting flood mitigation with other community benefits such as open space, recreation, and ecological function.

The reviewed literature also identifies important challenges. Voluntary buyout programs, as described by Siders (2018) and Vanucchi et al. (2025), typically produce scattered (checkerboard) patterns of acquisition over time, complicate comprehensive floodplain restoration, and leave many parcels in a state of incomplete ecological recovery — often maintained as mowed lawns rather than dynamic floodplain ecosystems. Equity concerns documented in the broader U.S. buyout literature — including unequal access to buyout offers depending on income and insurance status, and inadequate compensation for low-income homeowners — may be applicable to Portland's program context, though they are not directly documented for East Lents in the reviewed sources. The sources also caution against drawing firm conclusions about Portland-specific outcomes from the available evidence, as most detailed project data was not accessible in the reviewed corpus.

Case study: Queens (Queens, New York, United States)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Resilient Edgemere Community Planning Initiative (RECPI), Edgemere neighborhood, Rockaway Peninsula, Queens, New York City, New York, United States.

**Hazard(s):** Coastal flooding is the primary hazard. Superstorm Sandy (October 2012) caused catastrophic storm surge and flood damage in Edgemere, with flood depths of over six feet recorded along the shoreline (Olivotto et al., 2025). The neighborhood also experiences chronic "blue sky" flooding — nuisance ponding during normal weather conditions — caused by historical landfilling of surrounding marshlands, built-over creeks, and high groundwater (Olivotto et al., 2025). Sea level rise and increasing frequency and intensity of coastal storms further elevate long-term risk (Olivotto et al., 2025). All study sites in the broader New York area, including Edgemere, also experienced regular nuisance or "sunny day" flooding due to low-lying topography, high water tables, and existing infrastructure (Mockrin & Johnson, 2024).

**Type of Retreat:** A broader resilience and land-use planning initiative that included a limited voluntary buyout and acquisition component. The RECPI introduced zoning changes designating a Hazard Mitigation Zone (HMZ) that eliminates or limits new residential development in the most flood-exposed areas of the neighborhood. Seven property buyouts and acquisitions were completed as of September 2022, associated with NYC's post-Sandy recovery efforts (Olivotto et al., 2025). Olivotto et al. (2025) describe the bay-side area's current approach as consistent with a "soft, delayed retreat philosophy," whereby zoning changes mean that in the event of future catastrophic flooding, retreat may become the only viable option for remaining residents.

**Scale:** The neighborhood of Edgemere has a population of 8,885 (ACS 2015–2019, cited in Olivotto et al., 2025). Only 7 property buyouts and acquisitions were completed as of September 2022 (Olivotto et al., 2025; Mockrin & Johnson, 2024). The broader RECPI is neighborhood-wide, though its zoning and lot-management effects are spatially uneven.

**Key Actors:** New York City's Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) administered the buyout and acquisition program and owns most of the resulting vacant lots. The Mayor's Office of Resilience (MOR) co-led the RECPI. Community-based organizations active in the neighborhood include the Edgemere Community Civic Action (ECCA) and the Garden by the Bay community garden (Olivotto et al., 2025). A community-based organization (CBO) collaborated with researchers on community land visioning workshops (Olivotto et al., 2025). The New York State Governor's Office of Storm Recovery (GOSR) administered a separate state buyout program; the reviewed sources indicate GOSR buyouts were not completed in Edgemere, with the sources primarily discussing NYC-led efforts in this neighborhood (Mockrin & Johnson, 2024). The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) has a coastal storm risk management project planned for mid-Rockaway, still in design phase as of the review period (Olivotto et al., 2025).

**Timeline:** Superstorm Sandy struck October 29, 2012 (Mockrin & Johnson, 2024; Olivotto et al., 2025). The RECPI launched in 2015 as a multi-agency effort to address flood risk, post-Sandy recovery, and broader neighborhood conditions (Olivotto et al., 2025). Zoning changes, including the HMZ designation, followed. Seven property buyouts and acquisitions were completed between approximately 2015 and 2022. As of September 2022 (the latest field evidence in the reviewed sources), all 7 buyout and acquisition lots remained vacant; 6 were owned by HPD, and 1 had been transferred to the NYC Department of Parks and Recreation (Olivotto et al., 2025). Community land visioning workshops were held between November 2021 and March 2022 (Olivotto et al., 2025). The case remained ongoing in the latest reviewed evidence.

**Key Outcomes:** As of the review period, key outcomes include: (1) seven buyout and acquisition lots completed — all remained vacant as of September 2022, with residents reporting concerns about neglect, rodent infestation, and safety (Olivotto et al., 2025); (2) a Community Land Trust (CLT) was proposed as a possible governance mechanism for 119 city-owned vacant lots for affordable housing and community stewardship, with implementation remaining uncertain (Olivotto et al., 2025); (3) new mixed-use and market-rate residential development was proposed and/or advancing in other parts of the neighborhood, raising gentrification and climate-risk concerns among residents and the local community board (Olivotto et al., 2025); (4) persistent community distrust of city agencies, rooted in decades of unfulfilled urban renewal promises; and (5) the USACE has a $252,544,000 coastal storm risk management project planned for mid-Rockaway still in design phase (Olivotto et al., 2025, citing USACE, 2019, 2023).

---

### Narrative Summary

Edgemere is a predominantly Black and Hispanic, low-lying coastal neighborhood on the Rockaway Peninsula in Queens, New York City. According to the ACS 2015–2019 estimates cited in Olivotto et al. (2025), the neighborhood has a population of 8,885; 59.4% of residents identify as African American and 35% as Hispanic. The neighborhood has long been exposed to coastal flooding and, in October 2012, Superstorm Sandy caused severe damage — flood depths exceeding six feet were recorded along the shoreline, destroying homes and infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat, electricity, or with water damage (Olivotto et al., 2025). In the years following Sandy, the city launched the Resilient Edgemere Community Planning Initiative in 2015, a multi-agency effort intended to simultaneously reduce flood risk, support disaster recovery, and address decades of neighborhood disinvestment (Olivotto et al., 2025).

The RECPI represents a hybrid approach. On one hand, it introduced a Hazard Mitigation Zone that limits or prohibits new residential development in the most flood-prone areas near the bay, and the city completed 7 voluntary property buyouts and acquisitions associated with post-Sandy recovery. On the other hand, the city simultaneously advanced large-scale mixed-use and market-rate residential development on other parts of the neighborhood — framed by city officials as a strategy to bring services and affordable housing to a long-disinvested community, but criticized by residents and researchers as risking climate gentrification and failing to address core community needs (Olivotto et al., 2025). The development plan, when fully built, would bring 1,201 residential units (approximately 38% as affordable housing) and almost 150,000 square feet of retail space (Olivotto et al., 2025, citing City of New York, 2020). Community Board 14 presented a unanimous resolution calling for a moratorium on all upzoning requests until an environmental impact study addressed concerns that new developments were not aligned with existing services and neighborhood character (Olivotto et al., 2025).

As of September 2022, the seven completed buyout and acquisition lots remained vacant, with residents reporting concerns about neglect, rodent infestation, and safety (Olivotto et al., 2025). These realities are inseparable from a long history of racial housing discrimination, failed urban renewal, the closure of the local hospital, inadequate transportation and food access, and broken promises by city agencies dating back to the 1997 Urban Renewal Area designation (Olivotto et al., 2025). Residents — many of whom moved to Edgemere because it was one of the few places they could afford to buy a home in New York City — express strong place attachment alongside justified skepticism of government-led retreat and restoration programs. The literature suggests that managed retreat in a historically disinvested, majority-minority neighborhood cannot be fully understood without attending to the entangled histories of contextual injustice that shape residents' vulnerability, their distrust of institutions, and their capacity to engage meaningfully with adaptation planning (Olivotto et al., 2025).

Case study: Auckland (Auckland, Aukland Region, New Zealand)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Project Twin Streams (PTS), former Waitakere City (now part of Auckland Council), Auckland Region, Aotearoa New Zealand.

**Hazard(s):** Riverine and pluvial flooding. The project was developed in response to escalating flooding and stormwater management issues within the Twin Streams catchment (Opanuku and Waitītī streams).

**Type of Retreat:** Voluntary individual property buyout as part of a broader environmental restoration and stormwater management programme. The retreat component involved purchasing all or part of properties in the 100-year flood plain and removing houses to create stormwater reserves and management parks.

**Scale:** Approximately 156 property purchases were successfully negotiated (approximately half full purchases, half partial purchases such as land only). Approximately NZD $25 million was allocated to the property purchase phase, funded through a grant from Infrastructure Auckland, a public regional infrastructure development body. No population estimate is provided in the reviewed sources.

**Key Actors:** The former Waitakere City Council (now Auckland Council) was the primary implementing body. Funding was provided through Infrastructure Auckland. The Council deliberated chose not to use compulsory acquisition powers available under the Public Works Act 1981. The central government was not the primary funder or lead actor. The Waitakere City Council merged into Auckland Council in 2010; all events described occurred under the former Waitakere City Council.

**Timeline:** Project Twin Streams began in 2002 and was scheduled to run for approximately 10 years. The property purchase component was active throughout this period. At the time of the primary source (Vandenbeld and MacDonald, 2013), 156 property purchases had been successfully negotiated — language suggesting an ongoing or substantially completed acquisition phase rather than a formally closed post-retreat case.

**Key Outcomes:** The literature presents the managed-retreat component as a successful example of voluntary, carefully communicated acquisition. Land acquired was converted into stormwater reserves, management parks, cycle-ways, and walkways. Flood risk to residents was reduced and the ecological functioning of local waterways was improved. A small number of property owners chose not to sell; their flood risk was documented in Land Information Memoranda. The approach avoided protracted legal disputes — the voluntary, trust-based model allowed the Council to proceed without compulsory acquisition.

---

### Narrative Summary

Project Twin Streams (PTS) was conceived in response to chronic flooding and deteriorating stormwater management in the Twin Streams catchment of the former Waitakere City, Auckland. Rather than relying on hard engineering protection works, the Waitakere City Council developed a multi-objective programme combining environmental restoration, stormwater management, community development, cultural goals, and local employment creation. A central component was the voluntary purchase of properties within the 100-year flood plain and the removal of houses to create stormwater reserves, ecological parks, cycle-ways, and walkways.

The Council made a deliberate decision not to use compulsory acquisition powers available under the Public Works Act 1981. Instead, 156 property purchases were successfully negotiated on a voluntary basis. Properties were acquired at pre-announcement market valuations — used as a starting point for negotiation to prevent the Council from leveraging its interest in the property to depress the price — and the Council paid for moving costs and legal fees. The engagement process was carefully designed: nine months were spent developing consistent messaging and support materials before any contact was made with property owners. Council teams paired engineers who could explain flood risk with staff who had strong interpersonal skills, addressing both technical and emotional dimensions. Individual circumstances were recognised: for example, the Council agreed to purchase both houses in a case where a family lived in adjacent properties, and facilitated the relocation of special trees and the erection of plaques where properties had multi-generational significance.

The project framed the property acquisition positively — as an opportunity to help owners relocate away from flood hazard while improving the environmental, economic, social, and cultural wellbeing of the wider community through PTS. Those who relocated elsewhere in the area could still benefit from the parks and walkways created on vacated land, as well as the wider benefits of PTS. A small number of owners chose not to sell; flood risk was documented on their Land Information Memoranda. The literature presents this case as a notable example of how voluntary, carefully designed community engagement can achieve community acceptance of managed retreat without resorting to compulsion or protracted legal processes. Lawrence et al. (2020) cite Twin Streams alongside the Netherlands Delta Programme as a notable example of publicly funded pre-emptive managed retreat with dedicated funding and significant community engagement.

Case study: Linz (Linz, Danube floodplain, Austria)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Planned Relocation Program in the Eferding Basin and Machland North/South (Waves 1–2 and Wave 3), Upper Austria, along the Danube River, Austria (Global North).

**Hazard(s):** Riverine flooding from the Danube River. The region experiences severe and recurring flood events, with major documented floods in 1954, 1967, 2002, and 2013. Hydrological and geomorphological conditions in the central segment of the Eferding Basin mean that conventional flood protection cannot provide 100-year return period protection everywhere, making relocation the primary available risk reduction tool in those zones.

**Type of Retreat:** Voluntary property compensation/planned relocation. Homeowners in a designated relocation zone receive compensation for their buildings and demolition costs in exchange for permanently vacating and demolishing their structure. Land plots remain in private ownership but are rezoned to grassland with a permanent construction ban. The program operates as a subsidy/compensation scheme rather than a state property acquisition.

**Scale:** The program has unfolded across three waves from the 1970s to the present. Wave 1 (1970s–1991): approximately 40 households in Machland South, 100% relocated; Wave 2 (1991–2013): approximately 250 households in Machland North and South, near-100% relocated; Wave 3 (2013 announced, implemented from 2015 onward): approximately 150 households in the Eferding Basin targeted; by January 2021, 74 out of 152 households had accepted the relocation offer (approximately 40% acceptance), with 63 buildings fully demolished. The Eferding Basin comprises five municipalities: Alkoven, Feldkirchen, Goldwörth, Pupping, and Walding, in a 60 km² natural basin (figure stated in Seebauer et al. 2025 and Seebauer & Winkler 2020a).

**Key Actors:** The Federal Ministry for Transport, Innovation and Technology (BMVIT) played a central policy entrepreneurship role in Wave 2 and continues to provide up to 50% of total funding. The regional authority (State of Upper Austria) led Wave 3 design and implementation within a national-regional funding framework. Local authorities (municipalities/mayors) played mainly a communicative and facilitative role. Households are individually voluntary participants. The provided sources do not identify NGOs, First Nations/Indigenous communities, or international actors as involved in the governance structure.

**Timeline:** Wave 1 began in the 1970s, following earlier flood experiences; Wave 2 developed from the early 1990s following the 1991 flood and accelerated after 2002; Wave 3 was announced in October 2013, approximately four months after the June 2013 flood, and implemented from 2015 onward in the Eferding Basin. Planning and construction for technical flood defence in the remainder of the Eferding Basin also commenced in 2015 and is ongoing.

**Key Outcomes:** Waves 1 and 2 ultimately achieved very high acceptance over long timeframes. Wave 3 has achieved substantially lower acceptance (approximately 40% by 2021), partly attributed to a shortened five-year compensation window, insufficient pre-event community engagement, and a top-down implementation approach that generated mistrust and opposition. The relocation program successfully reduced hazard exposure for those households that relocated. In the related post-flood reconstruction context, households generally remodelled minimally after the 2013 flood, and the ambitions for climate resilience in building reconstruction were largely not realised (Seebauer et al. 2025). The program has been observed to involve limited procedural justice and partial compensation (80% of building value, no land compensation), which created financial barriers for some households.

---

### Narrative Summary

The Austrian Danube floodplain managed relocation program is one of the longest-running and most extensively documented voluntary planned relocation programs in Europe. Over more than five decades, three successive "waves" of relocation have moved hundreds of households away from sections of the Danube floodplain that cannot be protected through conventional structural flood defences. The program represents an evolving governance arrangement: beginning as an ad hoc local initiative in the 1970s, formalising into a nationally guided subsidy scheme in the 1990s, and reaching its current form after the major 2013 Danube flood that prompted Wave 3 in the Eferding Basin.

The program is voluntary: homeowners in designated relocation zones receive 80% of their building's appraised market value and 80% of demolition costs in exchange for permanently demolishing their structure and agreeing not to build again on the plot, which remains in their ownership but is rezoned to grassland. Households that decline the offer may remain but are subject to a construction ban and receive no public flood protection investment, and have experienced gradual withdrawal of communal services. The program is funded primarily by the national government (up to 50%) and the regional state authority (approximately 30%), with households contributing approximately 20%. Over time, the legal and procedural framework has become increasingly standardised, though local authorities and residents have had limited meaningful input into program design.

The case reveals important tensions between effective hazard risk reduction and broader social, procedural, and equity goals. Waves 1 and 2 achieved high acceptance rates largely because compensation windows remained open long enough to coincide with households' biographical circumstances (e.g., children leaving home, farm succession decisions), and because social learning effects — where early movers demonstrated feasibility — gradually normalised relocation. Wave 3, by contrast, was announced rapidly after the 2013 flood without prior local consultation. The relocation framework was subsequently amended after the initial announcement, contributing to mistrust, and a citizen protest initiative formed, though it ultimately did not shift the policy. Despite reducing flood exposure for those who moved, the program did not catalyse broader climate-resilient rebuilding: households that relocated rebuilt in new homes (which had to comply with energy efficiency standards but often featured larger floor areas, partially offsetting efficiency gains), while those who stayed generally made minimal building improvements. In the related reconstruction context, broader climate-resilience co-benefits were limited (Seebauer et al. 2025; Winkler et al. 2026). The case illustrates both the potential and the limitations of top-down, technically driven planned relocation as a long-term flood risk governance strategy in a western industrialised democracy.

Case study: Grantham (Grantham, Queensland, Australia)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

### Case Name and Location
Grantham Land-Swap Relocation; Grantham township, Lockyer Valley, Queensland, Australia. Grantham is described in the sources as a small rural town in the Lockyer Valley region of Queensland [Okada et al. 2018].

### Hazard(s)
Flash flooding caused by torrential rainfall in the surrounding mountains, resulting in inundation from Lockyer Creek on 10 January 2011 [Okada et al. 2018; Hsu et al. 2019; Brisbane Times 2020].

### Type of Retreat
Voluntary land-swap (relocation) program: the Lockyer Valley Regional Council (LVRC) offered flood-affected property owners the opportunity to exchange the title of their inundated land block for a new block of land on higher ground above the town, outside the flood zone. As a prior condition to acquiring land on the hill, participants were required to clear their land block by demolishing all existing buildings [Okada et al. 2018]. The program was branded "Strengthening Grantham" [Brisbane Times 2020].

### Scale
The land-swap was initially offered to the 119 Grantham and surrounding property owners whose houses were structurally damaged by the 2011 flood event [Okada et al. 2018]. Within the first two years, residents took up 86 lots [Brisbane Times 2020]. By early 2020, approximately 80–90 families lived in the relocated community on the hill [Brisbane Times 2020]. The LVRC purchased 378 hectares of higher land to develop the new community estate [Brisbane Times 2020]. Okada et al. (2018) list Grantham's population as 492 in Table 1.

### Key Actors
- **Lockyer Valley Regional Council (LVRC):** Initiating and implementing authority; the initiative was conceived by then-Mayor Steve Jones and implemented by LVRC [Okada et al. 2018; Brisbane Times 2020].
- **Jamie Simmonds (Environmental Engineer / Project Director):** Appointed as Project Director of "Strengthening Grantham"; drew on experience fast-tracking development applications and authored *Rising from the Flood: Moving the Town of Grantham* [Brisbane Times 2020].
- **Queensland State and Federal Governments:** Provided joint funding of AUD $18 million, mostly spent on land development of the resettlement blocks [Okada et al. 2018; Brisbane Times 2020].
- **Jude Munro (former CEO of Brisbane City Council):** Invited to help facilitate the masterplan workshops; described as having MC'd the workshops [Brisbane Times 2020].
- **Local residents:** Participated in workshops and land ballot processes; individual homeowners bore the costs of demolition and new construction [Okada et al. 2018; Brisbane Times 2020].
- **University of California Professor Nicholas Pinter:** Visited and documented the Grantham case; his contact with Simmonds prompted Simmonds to write his book [Brisbane Times 2020].

### Timeline
- **10 January 2011:** Flash flood event kills 12 people; 119 homes structurally damaged [Okada et al. 2018].
- **Late January / Early February 2011:** Mayor Jones conceives the relocation concept and the LVRC purchases higher land; Simmonds appointed Project Director within weeks of the flood [Brisbane Times 2020].
- **March 2011:** Land-swap program formally introduced [Okada et al. 2018].
- **Early 2011:** Community masterplan workshops held at Grantham State School [Brisbane Times 2020].
- **10 December 2011:** New Grantham officially opened (approximately 11 months after the flood); $18 million in state and federal funding expended [Brisbane Times 2020].
- **June 2012:** Community recovery centre closed, with the manager reportedly learning of the decision through the media [Okada et al. 2018].
- **June 2013:** Main measures completed [Okada et al. 2018, Table 1].
- **2016:** Mayor Steve Jones dies; local news source reports 634 people in the Grantham area [Brisbane Times 2020].
- **Early 2020:** Approximately 80–90 families in new Grantham; community described as stabilising but changed [Brisbane Times 2020].

### Key Outcomes
The land-swap program physically relocated approximately 86 lots/households to higher, flood-safe ground within approximately 11–12 months, at a cost of AUD $18 million [Okada et al. 2018; Brisbane Times 2020]. The program received domestic and international acclaim for its speed [Okada et al. 2018]. However, significant tensions and unresolved social issues accompanied this outcome. Not all flood-affected residents were able to participate — particularly those who could not afford demolition and construction costs, the elderly, and uninsured or under-insured households [Okada et al. 2018]. The community recovery centre, seen by some residents as a vital social support hub, was closed in June 2012; the manager reportedly learned of the decision through the media rather than directly from the LVRC [Okada et al. 2018]. Academic analyses consistently note that the LVRC's speed-focused, top-down approach left some vulnerable community members behind, and that the post-relocation community differs substantially in its social character from the pre-disaster one [Okada et al. 2018; Hsu et al. 2019].

### Narrative Summary

On 10 January 2011, the small Queensland town of Grantham was struck by a catastrophic flash flood that killed 12 people and structurally damaged 119 homes. On the night of the disaster, then-Mayor Steve Jones conceived what would become one of the most widely cited managed retreat projects in Australia. Within days, the Lockyer Valley Regional Council purchased more than 300 hectares of higher ground above the town — land belonging to a cattle property owner named Jimmy West, who was known to residents [Brisbane Times 2020] — and offered flood-affected homeowners a voluntary land swap: transfer the title of your damaged block to the Council, and receive a new block on the hill in exchange. The scheme was developed into a community master plan through a series of workshops held at the local school. Within approximately 11 months, the new Grantham on the hill was officially opened, funded by AUD $18 million from Queensland state and federal governments. By the first two years, 86 lots had been taken up; by early 2020, approximately 80–90 families had made the move.

By conventional measures of speed and physical risk reduction, Grantham is widely cited as a rapid managed retreat case. A visiting University of California researcher reportedly told the project director that a comparable project in the United States cost three times as much and took eight years [Brisbane Times 2020]. The relocation reduced flood exposure for participating households and allowed a relocated community to form. However, academic research and resident testimony reveal a more complicated picture. The speed that enabled the program's physical success also meant that residents had little time to process the trauma of the flood before being asked to make consequential, irreversible decisions. Okada et al. (2018) note that some residents stated the offer had been made too early for them to think and judge properly, as they were still in shock. Participation costs — demolition of old dwellings and construction of new ones — were too high for some residents, particularly the elderly and those without adequate insurance. One resident whose home was assessed as structurally standing received only a $20,000 ex gratia insurance payment and explained: "If someone gave me money today and said move up there today we would be up there quick. But the thing is, you had to have money" [Brisbane Times 2020]. Some households were left on the floodplain, unable to afford the move.

Perhaps most significantly, the LVRC's control over the recovery process came into direct conflict with the community recovery centre, which residents valued as an independent space for social support and mutual aid. The centre was closed in June 2012; the manager reportedly learned of the decision through the media rather than directly from the LVRC [Okada et al. 2018]. Academic accounts describe the Grantham land-swap project as successful in terms of risk mitigation and finance, but one that left some community members — often the most vulnerable — behind, and whose authority-driven, mitigation-focused strategy did not walk alongside community-based recovery [Okada et al. 2018]. The "new Grantham" that emerged is acknowledged, including by long-term residents, as a different community from the one that existed before: some original families sold their new lots and moved away; new residents moved in; familiar social fabric was disrupted [Brisbane Times 2020].

Case study: Valmeyer (Valmeyer, Illinois, United States)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Valmeyer, Illinois, United States (Monroe County, located five miles east of the Mississippi River, just south of St. Louis, Missouri)

**Hazard(s):** Riverine flooding from the Mississippi River, driven by levee breach. The town had also experienced flooding in 1910, 1943, 1944, and 1947, and the broader area had a long-standing floodplain designation established in the 1970s.

**Type of Retreat:** Wholesale community relocation — an extensive buyout and demolition of flood-damaged properties in "Old Valmeyer," combined with construction of an entirely new town on a bluff approximately 400 feet (120 metres) higher and about 1.5 miles (approximately 2.4 km) from the original site. This represents the most ambitious form of managed retreat documented in US floodplain management history: not simply property acquisition, but the relocation of most of the community and its core institutions, including residential, commercial, institutional, and infrastructure systems.

**Scale:** Pre-disaster population was approximately 897 (1990 Census). A total of 334 lots were purchased in the village of Valmeyer, and 494 parcels in total across Monroe County (including the village of Fults and unincorporated areas). Frequently cited narratives of successful relocation reference the acquisition of 302 residential properties, 29 businesses, and three churches. Approximately 60% of original inhabitants made the move to the new town. The project involved over 25 state, federal, and local agencies.

**Funding:** Funding estimates vary by scope and source. Valmeyer-specific buyout totals are reported at approximately $11.7 million for 334 lots; Monroe County buyout totals at approximately $18.6 million for 494 parcels. The total relocation cost for Valmeyer — including new town development — was approximately $31 million (reported by former Mayor Knobloch, as cited in Pinter 2021). Pinter (2021) estimates the per-person cost at approximately $70,000–$80,000 per resident who made the move. The funding structure for Monroe County buyouts involved FEMA HMGP at 50%, the Illinois Department of Commerce and Community Affairs and the National Flood Insurance Program at 25% each, with additional HUD CDBG funds and local borrowing for specific components such as mineral rights acquisition.

**Key Actors:** Local leadership was central — Mayor Dennis Knobloch (1989–1995) is widely credited as the primary champion, and both he and other community leaders have been credited with mobilizing relocation resources. Community participation occurred through seven 10-member citizen planning committees formed within the first 100 days after the flood. Key state and federal partners included FEMA (Hazard Mitigation Grant Program), the Illinois Department of Commerce and Community Affairs, the Illinois Emergency Management Agency, the Illinois Principals Association, the Economic Development Administration, the US Farmers Home Administration, and the Department of Energy Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy. HUD and the US Army Corps of Engineers played supporting roles.

**Timeline:** The Mississippi River breached Valmeyer's levee on August 1, 1993, flooding the village three separate times. Within six weeks, a survey by the Extension Office revealed about 60% of property owners wanted to leave. Community meetings and planning committees were formed within 100 days of the flood. The village signed a letter of intent to purchase a 500-acre farm parcel on the adjacent bluff. A November 1993 weekend "charrette" partnered regional architects and planners with community members to plan elements of the new town. The majority of buyout and demolition activity occurred between April 1994 and April 1996. The first family moved into New Valmeyer in April 1995; the new school was completed in April 1996. The village had paid off its relocation debt by 2002. The case is analyzed retrospectively as a post-relocation case, though formal long-term follow-up was limited.

**Key Outcomes:** The relocation removed the vast majority of residential and commercial structures from the floodplain. Flood-loss modelling by Pinter and Rees (2021) demonstrates that community relocation can reduce economic flood exposure by over 95%. New Valmeyer incorporated sustainable building technologies, including passive solar design, geothermal heat pumps, and energy-efficient construction, through the involvement of the DOE Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy. Population fell from 897 in 1990 to 496 in 1998, and later sources describe a substantial rebound — Pinter and Rees (2021) report the population rebounded to 140% of its pre-flood level, with Pinter (2021) citing approximately 1,263 people by 2010. However, 26 occupied pre-disaster residences chose to rebuild in Old Valmeyer, and approximately 40% of pre-flood residents did not relocate to New Valmeyer. About 75% of businesses did not survive the move, and planned commercial "Main Street" blocks in the new town were never completed. The quarry beneath the new town was converted into a warehouse complex housing the National Archives and Bluline Food Service, expanding the tax base. Social disruptions — lost businesses, fractured community networks, financial hardships — are documented but underreported relative to the physical success narrative.

---

### Narrative Summary

Valmeyer, Illinois, was a small farming community of approximately 900 residents located on the Mississippi River floodplain in Monroe County. On August 1, 1993, the Mississippi River breached the town's levee system, flooding the village three separate times. By FEMA standards, about 90% of buildings in Valmeyer were substantially damaged. Rather than rebuild in place — which would have required elevating all new structures 12–16 feet above flood levels at significant personal cost — local leaders and residents chose to relocate the community to a bluff approximately 400 feet higher and about 1.5 miles away. A survey conducted six weeks after the flood found about 60% of property owners wanted to leave. Driven by the objective of preserving the community and its tax base, Mayor Dennis Knobloch mobilized over 100 residents into seven 10-member citizen planning committees within the first 100 days. The village signed a letter of intent to purchase a 500-acre farm parcel on the adjacent blufftop. Approximately $31 million in federal and state funds — primarily through FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Grant Program — financed the acquisition, demolition, and construction of New Valmeyer, with the first residents moving in by April 1995.

The literature frequently describes Valmeyer as the "poster child" for wholesale community relocation as a flood mitigation strategy. In physical and demographic terms, the outcomes have been impressive: flood exposure was radically reduced, and later sources report that the population subsequently rebounded to exceed pre-disaster levels. New Valmeyer incorporated sustainable building technologies through DOE involvement. A quarry originally acquired to secure the new site's subsurface rights later became a commercially valuable warehouse complex, increasing the local tax base.

Yet scholars have also identified significant gaps in these success narratives. Approximately 40% of pre-flood residents did not relocate to New Valmeyer — some rebuilt on the old floodplain, others dispersed entirely. About 75% of pre-flood businesses failed to survive the move, and planned commercial blocks in the new town were never completed. Many residents found the compensation — while based on pre-flood market value — insufficient to pay off existing mortgages or cover the cost of a modern replacement home. The literature suggests renters and non-homeowners received less attention and are underrepresented in official accounts. Bureaucratic complexity, involving over 25 government agencies with sometimes conflicting regulations, caused delays and frustrated local leaders. The sense of community loss is documented but inadequately captured by dominant narratives of success that focus primarily on property removal, construction metrics, and federal funding utilization. As one resident described their new home: "I love the [new] town, …but it's not home" (Manda et al. 2023).

Case study: Seenigama (Seenigama, Southern Province, Sri Lanka)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Post-Tsunami Relocation/Resettlement — Southern Sri Lanka, with primary research sites in Galle District (Akmeemana Division), Hambantota District (New Town), Matara District (Kananke Watta/Talalla), and Seenigama, Southern Province, Sri Lanka.

**Hazard(s):** The 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami (primary trigger). The buffer zone regulation was also framed as a protection against future tsunamis and other coastal hazards (Fernando, 2018; Birkmann et al., 2026).

**Type of Retreat:** Post-disaster community relocation and resettlement. The government re-imposed coastal buffer zone regulations under the Coast Conservation Act No. 57 of 1981, prohibiting reconstruction of residential structures within 100 m of the sea. This compelled tens of thousands of affected households to relocate permanently to new settlements built inland. Two main program types operated simultaneously: a donor-driven (DD) approach, in which international NGOs and donors constructed houses on government-acquired land and transferred them to beneficiaries; and an owner-driven (OD) approach, in which government cash grants were provided to households with land outside the buffer zone to rebuild independently (Brookings-CMRD, 2015).

**Scale:** Nationally, the buffer zone regulation forced more than 70,000 tsunami-affected families to relocate (Fernando, 2018). National resettlement plans called for approximately 43,000 new houses on 387 sites outside the buffer zone across Sri Lanka (Ahmed & McEvoy, 2014). In the Galle District area, relocated settlements were situated approximately 8–15 km from the city center (Birkmann et al., 2026). Four documented settlements in Akmeemana Division (Salzburg: 79 units; Green Village: 90 units; China Charity Village: 135 units; Tea Garden: 92 units) totalled 396 housing units (Fernando, 2018, Table 1). Hambantota New Town comprised approximately 2,330 houses, the largest single post-tsunami resettlement project in Sri Lanka (Ahmed & McEvoy, 2014). The Kananke Watta sub-case in Matara District involved 18 households (Brookings-CMRD, 2015). The tsunami killed approximately 35,322 people in Sri Lanka and displaced approximately 480,000–516,150 individuals nationally (Brookings-CMRD, 2015).

**Key Actors:** Sri Lankan national government, including the Task Force for Rebuilding the Nation (TAFREN, established in February 2005/2006); the Tsunami Housing Reconstruction Unit (THRU) within the Urban Development Authority (UDA); the Ministry of Urban Development and Housing; and the Coast Conservation Department. At the local level, Divisional Secretariats and Grama Niladhari (village-level administrative officers) played central coordination roles. Key donors and NGOs included the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), USAID, Save the Children, Farms Lanka, Sewa Lanka, and the Institute for Development and Community Strengths (INDECOS). Academic researchers from the University of Colombo (Fernando), the University of Stuttgart (Birkmann), RMIT University (Ahmed & McEvoy), and the University of Moratuwa (Siriwardhana et al.) provided post-hoc evaluation (Fernando, 2018; Birkmann et al., 2026; Ahmed & McEvoy, 2014; Siriwardhana et al., 2021).

**Timeline:** The tsunami struck on 26 December 2004. Emergency evacuation and transitional shelter occurred immediately after, with families housed at temples, schools, and transitional camps in early 2005. The coastal buffer zone regulation was re-imposed in 2005 (Birkmann et al., 2026; Fernando, 2018). Buffer zone distances were subsequently modified — reduced from 100 m to 45 m in the Galle city area (Fernando, 2018) and, in the Kananke Watta/Matara area, from an initial 100–200 m to 35–55 m in early 2006 (Brookings-CMRD, 2015). Permanent relocation settlements were constructed in the years following the tsunami, with timing varying by site; the Kananke Watta families moved into permanent houses in June 2006 (Brookings-CMRD, 2015). Household surveys were conducted in the Galle area in 2005/2006 and 2007/2008, and again in 2024/2025 (Birkmann et al., 2026). The case is best described as in a long-term post-relocation phase, though systematic monitoring remains limited (Birkmann et al., 2026).

**Key Outcomes:** The outcomes are deeply mixed. About 58% of households interviewed in relocation sites in 2024/2025 considered their living conditions better compared to the first year after relocation; however, approximately half still reported continuous challenges in maintaining a livelihood (Birkmann et al., 2026). Some settlements had fewer than 40% of original beneficiaries remaining, with houses having been sold, rented, or vacated (Fernando, 2018). Key persistent problems include: distance from livelihoods (especially for fishing families); inadequate infrastructure and housing quality; legal title delays — households only received land title deeds after 10 years in the relocation site (Birkmann et al., 2026); erosion of community cohesion and conflicts with host communities (Fernando, 2018; Siriwardhana et al., 2021); and livelihood disruption. In the 2024/2025 survey, approximately 70% of households in the coastal zone considered the buffer zone regulation an inappropriate measure, compared to approximately 80% who viewed it as appropriate in 2005/2006 (Birkmann et al., 2026). Physical infrastructure has improved over time, particularly access to piped water and electricity, but long-term monitoring and institutional follow-up have been limited (Birkmann et al., 2026; Fernando, 2018).

---

### Narrative Summary

On 26 December 2004, a magnitude 9.3 earthquake in the Indian Ocean generated a tsunami that killed approximately 35,322 people in Sri Lanka and displaced an estimated 480,000–516,150 individuals (Brookings-CMRD, 2015). The southern coastal belt was among the most severely affected regions. In the immediate aftermath, the Sri Lankan government re-imposed an existing coastal buffer zone regulation under the Coast Conservation Act No. 57 of 1981, prohibiting reconstruction of residential buildings within 100 metres of the sea, and initiated resettlement programs to move affected families inland. This produced one of the largest post-disaster relocation programs in recent history, forcing more than 70,000 families to relocate (Fernando, 2018). National plans called for approximately 43,000 new houses on 387 sites outside the buffer zone (Ahmed & McEvoy, 2014). A national coordination body, TAFREN, was established in early 2005/2006 to coordinate donor assistance, while the Tsunami Housing Reconstruction Unit (THRU) within the Urban Development Authority oversaw two permanent housing programs: a donor-driven scheme for those displaced from the buffer zone, and an owner-driven scheme for those with land outside the zone (Birkmann et al., 2026). International donors — including the IFRC, USAID, and many other NGOs — funded and constructed new settlements on government-acquired land, primarily in rural areas far from the original coastal communities.

The relocation process was largely top-down and reactive. Affected families had minimal involvement in decisions about where they would be moved or how houses would be designed. Beneficiary selection was handled through local officials, including Grama Niladhari, and the sources report concerns about transparency and favoritism (Brookings-CMRD, 2015). The government's preference for state land when acquiring resettlement sites — driven by high private land prices — contributed to many relocation settlements being located in rural areas approximately 8–15 km from the Galle city centre (Birkmann et al., 2026). Housing quality was frequently poor, monitoring was inadequate, and neither donors nor government had a long-term adaptation plan for relocated communities (Fernando, 2018). The Kananke Watta sub-case in Matara District — where 18 families were relocated 1.5–2 km inland, funded entirely by the IFRC — illustrates the broader patterns: donor-driven construction on poorly assessed land, limited community involvement, and serious quality deficiencies (Brookings-CMRD, 2015).

Twenty years on, the picture is uneven. Physical infrastructure in relocation sites has improved, particularly in terms of access to piped water and electricity (Birkmann et al., 2026). Social integration with host communities has also increased, though it took many years (Birkmann et al., 2026; Siriwardhana et al., 2021). However, a substantial share of households continues to face poverty, inadequate transportation, and limited access to employment and services. Many original beneficiaries have sold or vacated their donated homes, and the buffer zone has been progressively reduced and is now widely viewed as inappropriate by coastal residents (Birkmann et al., 2026). The case offers important lessons about the long-term complexity of post-disaster relocation: that relocation is not a one-time event but a decades-long process requiring sustained institutional support, meaningful community participation, and adaptive management — none of which were sufficiently provided in this case.

Case study: Woodbridge Township (Woodbridge Township, New Jersey, United States)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

### Case Name and Location
**New Jersey Blue Acres Buyout Program — Watson-Crampton Neighbourhood, Woodbridge Township**
Woodbridge Township, Middlesex County, New Jersey, United States. As of the 2010 United States Census, Woodbridge had a total population of 99,585, making it the sixth-most-populous municipality in New Jersey at that time [Lakhwala 2022]. The Watson-Crampton neighbourhood is located in the area known as Woodbridge Proper, near downtown Woodbridge. The neighbourhood is bordered by the Woodbridge River to the east and the Wedgewood Brook to the north, and was historically surrounded by salt marshes, with many marshes still remaining in the area [Lakhwala 2022].

### Hazard(s)
The primary hazard is **flooding** — specifically riverine and pluvial flooding driven by proximity to the Woodbridge River and the surrounding wetland system. Woodbridge's location near the tidal strait Arthur Kill, the Raritan River, and the Rahway River, combined with low elevation (as low as five feet above sea level in some areas) and high impervious surface density, means the municipality experiences many types of flooding, including tidal and fluvial [Lakhwala 2022]. Roughly 19% of Woodbridge lies within a FEMA flood hazard area [Lakhwala 2022]. The Watson-Crampton neighbourhood is particularly exposed: a significant portion lies within FEMA's 100- and/or 500-year floodplain, and residents experienced repeated severe flooding during high tides, summer storms, and nor'easters, with significant impacts from Hurricane Irene (2011) and catastrophic impacts from Hurricane Sandy (October 2012) [Lakhwala 2022].

It should be noted that Hashida & Dundas (2024) characterize the successful Watson-Crampton buyouts as located along a street with creek flooding in an inland township, distinguishing Watson-Crampton from the ocean- or bay-shoreline coastal municipalities in New Jersey. Storm surge from Hurricane Sandy introduced coastal flooding mechanisms during that event, but the recurring hazard is primarily riverine and pluvial.

### Type of Retreat
**Voluntary individual property buyouts** under the New Jersey Blue Acres Program (NJBAP), administered by the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP). The program purchases eligible homes at pre-disaster fair market value. After acquisition, homes are demolished and land is permanently preserved as open space, accessible to the public for recreation or conservation [Lakhwala 2022; Hashida & Dundas 2024]. In Watson-Crampton, bought-out land has been the subject of a restoration project involving Rutgers University, using native plants to restore wetlands and create passive recreational space [Lakhwala 2022].

### Scale
- **Watson-Crampton neighbourhood-specific:** As of 2015, 121 applications had been received and 72 homes had closed transactions [Lakhwala 2022]. As of 2018, nearly 150 homes had been bought out in Watson-Crampton [Lakhwala 2022].
- **Woodbridge Township-wide:** Woodbridge Township supported 220 household applications and completed buyouts on 161 properties [Hashida & Dundas 2024]. As of 2021, over 160 homes in Woodbridge had been bought out and demolished [Lakhwala 2022].
- **Watson-Crampton population:** Approximately 1,500 residents lived in the neighbourhood at the time of the buyouts [Lakhwala 2022].
- **Program-wide:** The NJBAP completed 683 successful buyouts across 14 municipalities between 2013 and 2018 [Hashida & Dundas 2024]. As of 2020, Blue Acres had secured funding for 1,200 properties and demolished 700 [Shi et al. 2022].
- **Geographic scope:** A single neighbourhood within a larger township, with buyouts also occurring in other parts of Woodbridge.

### Key Actors
- **New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) / Blue Acres Program:** State administrator, led by Fawn McGee since 1995 [Shi et al. 2022; Lakhwala 2022].
- **Federal Government (FEMA and HUD):** Primary post-Sandy funders through HMGP and CDBG-DR [Hashida & Dundas 2024; Shi et al. 2022].
- **Woodbridge Township Government / Mayor John McCormac:** Local municipal partner, responsible for supporting applications, facilitating coordination, and assuming maintenance responsibility for bought-out lands [Hashida & Dundas 2024; Lakhwala 2022].
- **Sarah Brown (pseudonym):** A Watson-Crampton resident and teacher who played an important grassroots role by researching Blue Acres, going door-to-door, creating informational materials, and organizing community meetings that contributed to high application rates [Lakhwala 2022].
- **Rutgers University Cooperative Extension / NJ Agricultural Experiment Station:** Collaborated with the Township of Woodbridge on ecological restoration of bought-out parcels using native plants [Lakhwala 2022].
- **New Jersey voters:** Approved additional corporate business tax funding for the program in 2014 [Hashida & Dundas 2024].

### Timeline
- **1995:** Blue Acres established as an extension and partner of Green Acres to address flood-prone properties [Shi et al. 2022]; initial funding through three bond acts totalling $36 million [Shi et al. 2022].
- **October 2012:** Hurricane Sandy devastates Watson-Crampton and other Woodbridge neighbourhoods.
- **Early 2013:** New Jersey state government and FEMA funding commitments post-Sandy enable NJBAP to expand sharply; Watson-Crampton residents begin applying [Hashida & Dundas 2024].
- **2013–2014:** First round of buyouts processed in Watson-Crampton; Sarah Brown conducts community outreach; Blue Acres holds community meetings; Sarah Brown and her family complete buyout in 2014 [Lakhwala 2022].
- **2014:** New Jersey voters approve additional corporate business tax funding for the program [Hashida & Dundas 2024].
- **2015:** 121 applications received from Watson-Crampton; 72 homes closed [Lakhwala 2022].
- **2018:** Nearly 150 homes bought out in Watson-Crampton; wetland restoration underway; 683 total buyouts across 14 NJ municipalities from 2013–2018 [Lakhwala 2022; Hashida & Dundas 2024].
- **2021:** Over 160 homes in Woodbridge bought out and demolished [Lakhwala 2022].
- **Current status:** Ongoing/phased — land restoration is in progress, some households remain in the neighbourhood, and additional buyout rounds have been underway.

### Key Outcomes
- Watson-Crampton achieved a high rate of buyout participation relative to comparable communities, supported by grassroots organizing, municipal cooperation, and the standing Blue Acres program [Lakhwala 2022; Hashida & Dundas 2024].
- Bought-out land has been permanently preserved as open space, with a restoration project involving the Township of Woodbridge and Rutgers University using native plants to restore wetlands and create passive recreational space [Lakhwala 2022].
- Mayor McCormac reported that the Watson-Crampton neighbourhood experienced no flood issues during Hurricane Ida (2021), attributing this partly to bought-out plots now planted with water-absorbing species; he also reported that Woodbridge's tax base was not significantly impacted [Lakhwala 2022].
- Roughly half of Woodbridge buyout participants relocated within Woodbridge Township [Lakhwala 2022, Mayor McCormac interview].
- Participants experienced significant financial challenges (mortgage complications, moving costs, limited relocation assistance) and mental health impacts (stress during and after the process, anxiety during subsequent rain events) [Lakhwala 2022].
- Former residents reported loss of community ties and social networks post-relocation [Lakhwala 2022].
- The program is recognized as one of the few standing state-level buyout programs in the US, notable for its long institutional history, diversified in-house staff, and ability to handle complex cases [Shi et al. 2022; Hashida & Dundas 2024].
- Concerns persist regarding limited relocation assistance, absence of explicit social equity goals, insufficient psychosocial support, and limited tracking of where residents relocate [Shi et al. 2022; Siders 2019; Lakhwala 2022].

---

### Narrative Summary

The Watson-Crampton neighbourhood in Woodbridge Township, New Jersey, sits in a low-lying area bordered by the Woodbridge River and surrounded by wetlands, making it chronically susceptible to flooding. Residents endured repetitive flood events for years — including significant damage from Hurricane Irene in 2011 — but Hurricane Sandy in October 2012 proved to be a turning point. The storm surge pushed water from the overflowing Woodbridge River deep into the neighbourhood, inundating lower-lying homes along Crampton and Watson Avenues and convincing many residents that remaining posed an unacceptable and recurring risk. In the months that followed, a local resident — referred to in the research as "Sarah Brown," a pseudonym used by the thesis author — took it upon herself to research alternatives, learn about the Blue Acres Buyout Program, and systematically educate her neighbours. She went door-to-door, created informational flyers, and organized community meetings that brought in Blue Acres representatives to answer questions. This grassroots organizing was an important factor in Watson-Crampton achieving an unusually high rate of participation in the buyout program, alongside the municipality's active support and the standing institutional capacity of Blue Acres itself.

The New Jersey Blue Acres Program, established in 1995 and administered by the NJDEP as an extension and partner of the Green Acres open-space program, offered eligible homeowners the pre-Sandy (pre-disaster) fair market value of their homes. After Sandy, the program received a major infusion of federal FEMA and HUD funding — approximately $273 million — allowing it to expand dramatically. The process required both a voluntary homeowner application and active support from the municipal government. Woodbridge Township worked closely with residents to verify eligibility, facilitate the application process, and even created online maps so residents could see who had applied. Once acquired, homes were demolished, and land was permanently deed-restricted from residential development and preserved as open space. As of 2018, nearly 150 homes in Watson-Crampton had been bought out, with the land becoming the subject of an ecological restoration project by the Township of Woodbridge and Rutgers University, aimed at restoring wetlands and creating passive recreational space. Mayor McCormac reported that the neighbourhood experienced no flood issues during Hurricane Ida in 2021 and that the town's tax base was not significantly impacted by the buyouts.

Despite the program's relative success, participants faced significant challenges: mortgage complications and limited moving assistance created financial hardship; the uncertainty and drawn-out process produced mental health stress; and the dispersal of former neighbours eroded social networks. Blue Acres does not formally plan for receiving areas — homeowners receive buyout payments and must find replacement housing independently in the private market. Roughly half of Woodbridge buyout recipients relocated within the township, relying on the existing local housing market. Broader analyses of the program identify persistent equity concerns, including barriers for renters, non-citizens, and those with upside-down mortgages, as well as limited transparency in property selection criteria and insufficient psychosocial support. The Watson-Crampton case is nonetheless regarded as an example of how grassroots community leadership combined with a well-resourced, long-standing state program and active municipal support can achieve managed retreat at meaningful neighbourhood scale.
