Case study: Kinston (Kinston, North Carolina, United States)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Kinston-Lenoir County Floodplain Acquisition and Relocation Program, City of Kinston, Lenoir County, North Carolina, United States of America.

**Hazard(s):** Riverine flooding of the Neuse River floodplain, triggered by hurricanes and tropical storms. Hurricane Fran (September 1996) and Hurricane Floyd (September 1999) were the primary triggering events. Hurricane Bertha (July 1996) preceded Fran and caused minor wind damage and localized flooding; Hurricane Dennis (September 1999) saturated the drainage basin in the days before Floyd and contributed to the severity of that flood. Flooding was compounded by a technological hazard dimension: the Peachtree Wastewater Treatment Plant adjacent to Lincoln City flooded during both storms, releasing raw and partially treated sewage into the Neuse River, and six junkyards in the floodplain spilled oils, chemicals, and other toxic compounds into floodwaters.

**Type of Retreat:** Voluntary individual property buyout and relocation program. Individual homeowners in the 100-year floodplain were offered pre-disaster fair market value for their homes, primarily through FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP), supplemented by North Carolina's State Acquisition and Relocation Fund (SARF) to assist residents in purchasing replacement housing within city limits. The program operated as voluntary acquisition; officials did not pursue eminent domain, noting it was not a viable option and would have disqualified the city from HMGP funds.

**Scale:** Approximately 775 individual property acquisitions within the city of Kinston, totaling an estimated 1,500–2,000 people displaced from the floodplain, representing approximately 7% of Kinston's total population at the time. The FEMA case study reports that Kinston and Lenoir County together acquired over 1,000 properties with HMGP funds, with approximately 225 remaining to be acquired at the time of that publication. The buyout area was concentrated in the southern portion of Kinston, including Lincoln City and adjacent floodplain neighborhoods. Virtually all of the residents bought out were African American, with large concentrations of low-income and elderly populations.

**Key Actors:** City of Kinston planning department (led by Floodplain Administrator Tommy Lee); Lenoir County government; the County Hazard Mitigation Planning Team (COHMIT); North Carolina Division of Emergency Management (administering HMGP); North Carolina Division of Community Assistance (administering SARF and Community Development Block Grants); U.S. FEMA; U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD, via CDBG); the Greater Kinston Community Development Corporation (GKCDC), a local non-profit; the Conservation Fund; the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill; the Kinston Area Recovery Effort (KARE) volunteer organization; and real estate professionals who helped residents find replacement housing.

**Timeline:** Hurricane Fran struck September 1996. COHMIT was formed within 30 days. HMGP applications were submitted December 1996, but the first grant was not processed until 14 months later. The first property acquisition occurred April 1998. Hurricane Floyd struck September 1999. The Greater Kinston Urban Growth Plan was formally adopted October 1999. After Floyd, a pre-disaster application package was submitted and approved within one week. The buyout program continued through approximately 2004. A Clean Water Management Trust Fund grant to acquire remaining vacant lots in the floodplain was received around 2005. Green infrastructure planning continued through at least 2005–2006. By the time of the reviewed sources, the bulk of acquisitions were complete, though vacant-lot acquisition and Green Infrastructure Plan implementation were still ongoing.

**Key Outcomes:** The program achieved a 97% participation rate among eligible homeowners. Approximately 90% of participants relocated within Kinston city limits; according to McCann (2006), this created a net tax gain for the city because equity on new homes was generally substantially higher than on the flooded properties. The first 101 acquired buildings avoided an estimated $6,387,000 in flood losses during Hurricane Floyd (McCann 2006, Table 1). Over $100 million in grant money was administered overall (McCann 2006), though the precise breakdown across funding streams is not fully reconciled in the available sources. Beyond the buyout itself, the city used disaster recovery funding to advance broader smart-growth goals: construction of 170 single-family homes on infill lots; rehabilitation of an abandoned high school into 57 units of senior housing (Grainger Place) plus 100 additional multi-family units; a downtown business incubator (Kinston Enterprise Center); removal of five of six floodplain junkyards; and decommissioning of the Peachtree Wastewater Treatment Plant. A Green Infrastructure Plan was developed for the acquired open space in partnership with Lenoir County, the Conservation Fund, and UNC Chapel Hill. However, the program carries critical equity dimensions: buyouts were concentrated almost entirely in historically Black, low-income neighborhoods. A post-buyout episode — in which some homes acquired after Floyd were refurbished and relocated into other African-American neighborhoods without notifying original homeowners or, according to the Johnsons, nearby residents — revealed major gaps in notification, accountability, and care in the program's devolved governance structure (de Vries and Fraser 2017).

---

**Narrative Summary**

Kinston, North Carolina, a small city of approximately 20,000 people in Lenoir County, experienced two devastating hurricanes within three years — Fran in 1996 and Floyd in 1999. Both storms caused the Neuse River to overflow its banks and flood significant portions of the city's southern neighborhoods, which were predominantly low-income, African-American areas located in the floodplain. Floyd, which deposited over 13 inches of rain in 24 hours and caused the Neuse to crest more than 10 feet above flood stage, compounded damage from a still-incomplete recovery from Fran. A key factor in both floods was a compound hazard: the Peachtree Wastewater Treatment Plant, located adjacent to the Lincoln City neighborhood, flooded during both storms, releasing raw and partially treated sewage, and six junkyards in the floodplain spilled oils and other toxic compounds into floodwaters. The fecal contamination that entered Lincoln City homes during Floyd was described by de Vries and Fraser (2017) as a defining factor in residents' willingness to participate in the buyout.

In response, the City of Kinston — with state and federal partners — implemented a voluntary floodplain buyout and relocation program funded primarily through FEMA's HMGP (75% of acquisition costs), Community Development Block Grants (HUD), and North Carolina's SARF. The program achieved a 97% participation rate among eligible homeowners, moving approximately 1,500–2,000 residents out of the floodplain, approximately 90% of whom relocated within the city. Kinston distinguished itself from comparable communities by integrating the buyout not merely as a risk-reduction measure but as the implementation vehicle for a broader urban growth plan, incorporating affordable housing, downtown revitalization, environmental hazard removal, and green infrastructure planning. The acquired floodplain is now largely open space, with forest regrowth across much of the area, though some vacant lots, remaining structures, and utilities are still present.

Despite these widely cited achievements, the case carries important critical dimensions. The buyout was concentrated almost entirely in historically Black, low-income neighborhoods that had been confined to flood-prone land since the early twentieth century due to racial segregation. De Vries and Fraser (2017) document a post-buyout episode in which some homes acquired after Floyd — which had been contaminated with sewage — were refurbished by the Greater Kinston Community Development Corporation and relocated into other African-American neighborhoods in Kinston, without notifying the original homeowners or, according to the Johnsons, nearby residents in receiving areas. Residents who raised concerns found no accountability at the city, state, or federal level, with FEMA indicating the matter was outside its jurisdiction. This episode illustrates how the program's devolved governance structure and its "logic of choice" — where responsibilities were demarcated contractually — perpetuated rather than remedied the discriminatory waterscape dynamics that originally produced the hazard conditions in Lincoln City. The Kinston case thus stands simultaneously as a frequently cited model of successful floodplain acquisition and as a critical case study in the equity limitations of devolved managed retreat governance.

Case study: Chennai (Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Post-Tsunami Resettlement of Coastal Fishing Communities, Coromandel Coast, Tamil Nadu, India. Primary case sites are nine fishing villages located along the Coromandel Coast in Thiruvallur, Kanchipuram, Villupuram, and Nagapattinam districts of Tamil Nadu, plus the Srinivasapuram neighbourhood of Chennai, Tamil Nadu. Comparative case sites are Hambantota New Town, Hambantota town, and Seenigama in Southern Sri Lanka. Note: The Sri Lanka and India programmes operated under distinct regulatory frameworks and are treated as related but separate contexts throughout this document.

**Hazard(s):** The Indian Ocean Tsunami of 26 December 2004.

**Type of Retreat:** Community-level resettlement — the relocation of entire or partial fishing settlements to newly constructed inland housing. In Tamil Nadu, this was implemented through a public–private partnership in which state government provided land and NGOs constructed standardized housing. In Sri Lanka, a post-tsunami buffer zone policy restricting rebuilding along the coast led to plans for new settlements on land outside the buffer zone, funded by international and local NGOs and philanthropic organizations, with land donated by government or purchased by NGOs. In Chennai (Srinivasapuram), the government proposed relocating fishing families approximately 22 km away, but strong community resistance delayed any permanent construction.

**Scale:** Across Tamil Nadu, the Tsunami Rehabilitation Programme proposed the construction of 84,542 houses (government: 47,491; NGO: 37,051); approximately 45,035 were completed. The paper by Bavinck et al. (2015) reports 686,069 hectares of housing land acquired, though the table note indicates this figure does not distinguish government- and NGO-procured land. The nine Coromandel Coast case study villages varied widely in size, from small hamlets to larger fishing settlements; Akkaraipettai, the largest site, saw approximately 768 houses constructed by the Tata Relief Committee for some 3,500 people, while the smallest studied site (Nemmeli Kuppam) comprised 42 houses. In Srinivasapuram, Chennai, according to a survey of the Tamil Nadu Slum Clearance Board (TNSCB), 769 families out of a total of 3,086 families in the area belonged to the fishing community; 54 people died in the tsunami. In Sri Lanka, more than a million people were affected overall, nearly 90,000 houses were completely or partially damaged, and plans were made to build 43,000 new houses on 387 sites outside the buffer zone; Hambantota New Town alone comprised 2,330 houses.

**Key Actors:**
- *Tamil Nadu (Coromandel Coast sites)*: Government of Tamil Nadu (district authorities, Revenue Administration, Disaster Management and Mitigation Department) provided land and issued GO 172 (March 2005) and CRZ-based guidelines. Different NGOs were responsible for construction at each site: Madras Social Society Service (MSSS) in Sathankuppam; Evangelical Church of India (ECI) and Government in Karikattukuppam; Village Community Development Society (VCDS) and World Vision in Mandavai Pudukuppam; Joyce Meyer Ministries (JMM) and YMCA Salem in Koonimedu Kuppam; Lutheran World Service (LWS) and Billy Graham Evangelical Association (BGEA) in Anichan Kuppam; Amma Foundation/Trust in Samanthaipettai; Tata Relief Committee (TRC) in Akkaraipettai; World Vision in Kallar. Caste panchayats played an important intermediary role in several sites.
- *Chennai (Srinivasapuram)*: Tamil Nadu Slum Clearance Board (TNSCB) was the agency responsible for tsunami housing reconstruction. UNTRS (United Nations Team for Recovery Support), mentioned in Raju (2013) as a UN coordination body for tsunami recovery activities in Tamil Nadu, was among stakeholders interviewed. NGOs operating in the field opposed the proposed relocation.
- *Sri Lanka*: Various international and local NGOs, philanthropic, political and religious organizations implemented housing in Hambantota New Town (on government-donated land); a local NGO implemented programmes in Seenigama (on privately purchased land). The research on Sri Lanka and Chennai was supported by Australian Research Council (ARC) funding and further informed by an AusAID-funded study.

**Timeline:** Tsunami: 26 December 2004. Emergency relief and initial planning: January–March 2005. Government of Tamil Nadu GO 172 issued: 30 March 2005. Construction of new settlements underway in most Tamil Nadu sites: 2005–2007, with some sites (e.g., Karikattukuppam) still under construction as of 2008–2010. The fastest completion was Samanthaipettai, where residents received keys before Christmas 2005, approximately six months after the tsunami. Field research by Bavinck et al.: April–June 2008. Data collection for the Raju (2013) study in Srinivasapuram: May 2008. As of May 2008, four years after the tsunami, the Chennai community and state were still debating and negotiating relocation, and no permanent housing had been constructed for Srinivasapuram residents.

**Key Outcomes:** Approximately 45,035 houses were completed across Tamil Nadu under the programme. Many fisher households expressed satisfaction with the physical quality of new concrete houses compared to earlier thatch or self-built structures, and with basic infrastructure improvements (electricity, water, connecting roads) in some sites. However, the distance of new settlements from the shoreline was widely perceived as impairing fishing livelihoods — an impediment to monitoring sea conditions, launching boats, drying nets, and storing equipment. In several sites (notably Samanthaipettai), some households moved back to the old settlement or maintained partial residence in both locations. In Kallar, where the new settlement was built six kilometres inland, fishers faced severe livelihood disruption; women who relocated to New Kallar generally lost income-generating opportunities they had previously held in fisheries. Community participation in house design and allocation was limited in most sites. Random allocation of houses disrupted existing social ties in some communities. In Srinivasapuram, Chennai, community resistance delayed housing reconstruction significantly; as of the research period (2008), no permanent housing had been built and residents were living in damaged buildings or self-constructed temporary shelters. In Sri Lanka, infrastructure deficiencies (drainage, water supply, sanitation, transport, security) were common in new settlements, and some beneficiaries had abandoned, leased, or transferred their properties.

**Narrative Summary:**

When the Indian Ocean Tsunami struck on 26 December 2004, it devastated fishing communities across Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka, destroying houses, boats, and equipment and killing thousands. The Tamil Nadu state government and a wide array of NGOs responded by constructing new housing settlements inland, using the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) 1991 Notification — originally an environmental protection instrument — as the legal basis for relocating communities away from the coast. Government Order 172 of March 2005 guided this process, recommending that new settlements be located at least 500 metres from the High Tide Line. By the time of the primary research fieldwork in 2008, over 45,000 houses had been completed under the Tamil Nadu programme, and Sri Lanka had embarked on plans for 43,000 new houses on 387 sites outside its post-tsunami buffer zone.

However, outcomes across the studied sites reveal a persistent gap between the safety rationale advanced by the state and the livelihood realities of fishing communities. Fisher households depend on proximity to the sea for their economic survival — to monitor weather and sea conditions, launch boats, dry and store nets and gear, and sell or process fish along the shoreline. Relocating settlements hundreds of metres or even kilometres from the shore disrupted these practices substantially. In several Tamil Nadu sites, families moved back to the old coastal location, maintained dual residences, or rented out their new houses rather than occupying them. In Kallar, where authorities placed the new settlement six kilometres inland, fishers faced the most extreme livelihood disruption; women who relocated lost income-generating opportunities in fisheries. In Srinivasapuram, Chennai, the community's organized resistance to a proposed relocation 22 kilometres away blocked the process entirely, leaving residents in damaged or temporary structures four years after the disaster.

The planning process was broadly characterized by top-down decision-making, limited community consultation, and standardized house designs imposed without reference to fishing household needs. Infrastructure provision was frequently inadequate or delayed in both India and Sri Lanka — drainage, water supply, sanitation, and transport links all presented serious problems in many new settlements. Where caste panchayats were cohesive and widely recognized, as in Sathankuppam and Anichan Kuppam, communities fared better in negotiating outcomes; where panchayat legitimacy was contested, as in Koonimedu Kuppam, the process was delayed and less satisfactory. Critics, including NGO representatives interviewed in Chennai, argued that the tsunami was used as a trigger to relocate fishing communities from the coast on the pretext of safety — a view echoed in academic commentary linking the process to "disaster capitalism." Questions about the future of coastal land rights and the sustainability of relocated communities remained unresolved as of the research period.

Case study: Iloilo (Iloilo, Western Visayas Region, Philippines)
Section: Case Study Overview (Summary)

**Case Name and Location:** Iloilo Flood Control Project (IFCP) Resettlement — Iloilo City, Western Visayas, Philippines (Global South)

**Hazard(s):** Riverine and pluvial flooding, with typhoons serving as acute triggers and climate change providing broader adaptation context (including sea-level rise and coastal flooding risk). [See et al., 2023; See and Wilmsen, 2020; WRI, 2023]

**Type of Retreat:** The IFCP is analyzed in the academic literature as climate-induced displacement and resettlement (CIDR). Mainstream IFCP relocation was largely involuntary — relocatees did not have the option to stay in situ because the land was claimed by the government as flood-prone. A parallel, community-driven housing initiative led by the Homeless People's Federation of the Philippines Inc. (HPFPI) operated alongside the IFCP and involved a more participatory, community-organized process. [See et al., 2023; See and Wilmsen, 2020]

**Scale:** Approximately 3,500 households were identified for resettlement as part of the IFCP, the majority of whom lived below the poverty line. [See et al., 2023] The primary resettlement site is a 16.2-hectare parcel in San Isidro. [See et al., 2023; WRI, 2023] The HPFPI-led participatory housing component has supported approximately 1,250 households across 23 city sites. [WRI, 2023] By 2009, an estimated 9,700 households were living in informal settlements citywide with no formal tenure. [WRI, 2023] Iloilo City has a population of approximately 500,000. [See and Wilmsen, 2020]

**Key Actors:** The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH); Iloilo City government (including the Iloilo City Urban Poor Affairs Office/ICUPAO, City Social Welfare and Development Office, City Engineers' Office, City Planning and Development, and City Health Office); the National Housing Authority; four NGOs funded by development agencies based in Europe and the United States (referred to as NGOs A, B, C, and D); the Homeless People's Federation of the Philippines Inc. (HPFPI); the Iloilo City Urban Poor Network (ICUPN); the Asian Development Bank (ADB); and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA). [See et al., 2023; WRI, 2023]

**Timeline:** The IFCP began in 2002. [See et al., 2023] The Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) was drafted by DPWH in 2005. [See et al., 2023; DPWH, 2005] Mayor Jerry P. Treñas was elected in 2001 and committed early to community engagement and government-banked land for resettlement. [WRI, 2023] HPFPI co-founded the Iloilo City Urban Poor Network (ICUPN) in 2005, and conducted citywide surveys from 2007 onward. [WRI, 2023] A pivotal event was Typhoon Fengshen in 2008, which flooded 152 of Iloilo's 180 barangays and submerged about 80% of the city, displacing thousands of families and increasing the urgency of resettlement. [See and Wilmsen, 2020; WRI, 2023] Fieldwork assessing outcomes was conducted in 2018. [See et al., 2023] The national government subsequently indicated its intention to use Iloilo's resettlement program as a model for other adaptation projects in the Philippines. [See et al., 2023]

**Key Outcomes:** Commentators and officials have described the IFCP as a participatory success story, and the national government has cited it as a model for adaptation projects in the Philippines. [See et al., 2023; See and Wilmsen, 2020] However, detailed empirical research conducted in 2018 reveals significant procedural and distributive inequities. Resettlement outcomes varied sharply depending on which NGO managed the relocation. Households managed by NGO A — selected partly on the basis of higher incomes and capacity to service housing loans, and, according to interviewees, partly through political connections — experienced better housing quality, improved basic services, and income growth. By contrast, households managed by NGOs B, C, and D received free but inferior prefabricated housing, inadequate water and sanitation, and minimal post-resettlement support. Post-resettlement income inequality worsened. The IFCP was guided by an RAP that incorporated several international safeguard elements, though important best-practice features were missing or weakly implemented. [See et al., 2023; See and Wilmsen, 2020] The HPFPI-led community savings and housing approach generated better participatory and livelihood outcomes for its participants. [See et al., 2023; WRI, 2023]

---

**Narrative Summary**

Iloilo City is a low-lying urban centre of roughly 500,000 people on Panay Island in the Philippines. Traversed by three major rivers and situated only 2.6 metres above sea level on a flat alluvial plain, the city faces chronic and severe flooding. [See et al., 2023; See and Wilmsen, 2020] Beginning in 2002, the Iloilo Flood Control Project was launched as a large infrastructure initiative designed to protect the city against floods of up to a one-in-twenty-year return period. [See et al., 2023] A central component of this project required the resettlement of approximately 3,500 low-income households living along the waterways — the majority below the poverty line — to a 16.2-hectare site at San Isidro. [See et al., 2023] The urgency of action was sharpened in 2008 when Typhoon Fengshen flooded 152 of Iloilo's 180 barangays and submerged about 80% of the city, displacing thousands of families. [See and Wilmsen, 2020; WRI, 2023] Climate change, including rising sea levels and increasing coastal flooding risk, provides the broader adaptation context for the project, though the IFCP itself was primarily centered on addressing flood risk from the city's waterways and typhoon events. [See et al., 2023]

The IFCP resettlement was formally guided by a Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) developed by DPWH, designed to comply with ADB and World Bank social safeguard standards. [See et al., 2023] Four NGOs funded by development agencies based in Europe and the United States were engaged to manage housing construction and relocation. [See et al., 2023] In parallel, the Homeless People's Federation of the Philippines (HPFPI) developed a community-driven approach, organizing savings groups, conducting citywide surveys, and working with city government to develop a broader Participatory Housing and Urban Development program across 23 city sites. [WRI, 2023] The election of Mayor Jerry P. Treñas in 2001 was a turning point: as early as 2002, the city committed to purchasing land for within-city relocations and involving urban poor communities in site selection and planning. [WRI, 2023]

Despite the project's positive reputation, empirical research conducted in 2018 reveals a more troubled picture. The IFCP was guided by an RAP that incorporated several international safeguard elements, though important best-practice features were missing or weakly implemented — including no options assessment, no distributional analysis, no independent review panels, and no performance bonds. [See et al., 2023] Participation in decision-making was uneven: households managed by NGO A, which required loan repayment capacity and offered training, reported far greater involvement in planning and experienced significantly better housing quality, services, and income growth. Households managed by NGOs B, C, and D received free but inferior prefabricated housing and minimal post-resettlement support. Interviewees reported political interference, including requests to admit non-eligible beneficiaries into NGO A's program. [See et al., 2023] The result was that pre-existing socioeconomic inequalities were replicated and often deepened by the resettlement process, despite its stated commitment to equitable outcomes. The HPFPI's complementary community-led work — including community savings schemes, innovative financing, and collaborative governance — demonstrates that more participatory and equitable outcomes are achievable when communities are genuinely empowered. [See et al., 2023; WRI, 2023]
